Given a user query and retrieved candidates, MemChain first generates a question-conditioned evidence plan, then constructs an ordered grounded evidence trace that organizes retrieved memories according to their semantic roles and dependencies, and finally executes explicit memory actions to produce a concise evidence context for answer generation. To train the mediator, we introduce a two-stage learning framework. Supervised trace learning first teaches the policy to generate structurally valid plans, traces, actions, and evidence contexts. We then propose Trace-Guided Memory Policy Optimization (TMPO), a reinforcement learning objective that optimizes the memory policy using downstream answer quality while jointly encouraging trace grounding, evidence support, structural validity, and answer stability across multiple rollouts. Experiments on LoCoMo and LongMemEval-

78be9bdcbce9cf3f83970586.title_original: PATH-Bench: Path-Dependent Evaluation of Lifelong Agents
78be9bdcbce9cf3f83970586.excerpt: arXiv:2608.01149v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Lifelong LLM agents increasingly adapt through external learning states that store past interactions as retrievable memories or reusable skills, yet existing benchmarks rarely account for how the path of accumulated experience shapes what agents transfer and retain. In this work, we establish PATH-Bench, a benchmark for path-dependent evaluation of lifelong agents. PATH-Bench estimates directed task relationships via multi-model in-context learning, constructs probe-centered sequences with controlled helpful and interfering histories, and repeatedly evaluates probe tasks to measure average performance, forward transfer, backward transfer, and forgetting. We evaluate eight representative agents on single-turn code generation and multi-turn tool-use tasks under positive- and negative-dominant histories. Benchmark results show that experience utility depends jointly on how experience is represented and on the task's interaction structure, that strong transfer does not ensure retention, and that later experience can reshape gains acquired earlier in the learning path. Based on these findings, we propose Selective Experience Use (SEU), an agent harness that regulates how path-accumulated experience influences each new task, admitting helpful items while filtering out potential interference. SEU consistently reduces forgetting while improving forward transfer in the majority of settings. The PATH-Bench provides both a controlled e

9b16a42aee626bbe8398bea6.title_original: Flow-by-Flow:Content-Judgment Bypass for Governing AI Output in High-Loss Domains
9b16a42aee626bbe8398bea6.excerpt: arXiv:2608.07474v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Human review is a load-bearing safeguard in AI governance: oversight mandates such as Article 14 of the EU AI Act presume that accountable reviewers can scrutinize what they approve. In high-loss domains open to any submitter, such as patent examination, litigation and peer review, generative AI allows the number of submissions and the review effort each requires to grow faster than review capacity. This paper asks how institutions can keep this supervisory load within capacity without judging content, since content judgment either reintroduces hallucination risk or consumes scarce review capacity. Treating supervisory load as submission volume times per-item load, we show that if it grows at a compound rate while capacity grows linearly, capacity is exceeded in finite time; added capacity or one-off load reductions postpone exceedance only logarithmically, whereas lowering the growth rate postpones it hyperbolically. We then propose Flow-by-Flow, which prices supervisory load from countable features of submissions and caps the load admitted for review. We derive four requirements for any pathway that admits submissions beyond the cap and show that they can be met jointly, using identity-bound waiting as an existence proof whose ethical costs call for better implementations. In an uncertainty analysis under assumed parameter ranges, the design postpones capacity exceedance by a median of three years relative to supervision e

c0c68b2bf763c889c2a36e14.title_original: KGCache: Amortized Subgraph Retrieval for KG Reasoning with LLMs
c0c68b2bf763c889c2a36e14.excerpt: arXiv:2608.07954v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models can answer knowledge-intensive questions more reliably when they are grounded with knowledge graphs, but systems such as Think-on-Graph and Reasoning-on-Graph repeatedly query the same graph neighborhoods across different questions. In this work, we study this repeated retrieval in Knowledge Graph Question Answering~(KGQA) workloads and propose KGCache, an in-memory cache for one-hop knowledge graph neighborhoods. KGCache is designed to be compatible with both iterative traversal (ToG) and one shot planning (RoG) KGQA paradigms. KGCache is placed between the KGQA engine and the backend serving the KG, so repeated entity requests can be served from cache instead of issuing new KG queries. We evaluate KGCache on WebQSP and CWQ using LRU, LFU, and a trace-aware Oracle policy. Our analysis shows that both datasets contain substantial entity reuse among starting entities and entities reached during traversal. We also explore semantic caching for similar queries, which shows additional hit-rate gains on WebQSP and needs further accuracy testing on CWQ. Entity caching accelerates KG retrieval by up to $1.91\times$, while semantic-context caching achieves up to $1.08\times$ full-system speedup in the evaluated configurations, with each hit being up to $17.98\times$ faster. End-to-end gains are bounded by the share of runtime spent on KG retrieval, so caching is most beneficial when KG access is slow, e.g., with

dd59e3f644425837c503e180.title_original: Do LLM Agents Negotiate Rationally? A Mechanism-Design Framework for Verifiable Multi-Agent Interaction over A2A/MCP
dd59e3f644425837c503e180.excerpt: arXiv:2608.14613v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Modern LLM-agent frameworks increasingly interoperate through standards such as Anthropic's Model Context Protocol (MCP) for agent-to-tool access and Google's Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol for agent delegation and negotiation. However, these protocols specify transport and discovery rather than strategic correctness and do not guarantee efficient, individually rational, or strategy-proof outcomes. We introduce a framework that (i) encodes classical negotiation mechanisms, including alternating-offers bargaining and Vickrey-Clarke-Groves-style auctions, as constraints over A2A message schemas; (ii) provides a lightweight runtime verification and repair layer that checks messages against protocol invariants; and (iii) offers a benchmark of negotiation and allocation tasks with known optimal solutions for measuring deviations from game-theoretic predictions. We evaluate multiple LLM backbones using unstructured dialogue, structured protocols, and structured protocols with verification. Across negotiation trials (N=30 per condition), verification reduces outcome variance, while structured protocols achieve 100 percent success for both models. After correcting parser artifacts, audited unstructured baselines achieve approximately 97 percent and 93.3 percent success. In auction experiments (N=30 per model), both models achieve 100 percent efficient allocation but differ sharply in truthful bidding: one bids its exact valuation in eve

6abe83c7e2112ad0445500d1.title_original: Competing at Every Price Point with Agentic Evolution over a Menu of LLMs
6abe83c7e2112ad0445500d1.excerpt: arXiv:2608.16207v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Consider a firm that surveys its competition for a particular agentic task and seeks to offer superior accuracy at every price point. A firm that Pareto-dominated its competitors would leave no rational customer a reason to buy elsewhere. This paper shows a path to this kind of capability by evolving multi-LLM Python agents from training pools of at most 100 examples. Given a priced menu of nine LLM endpoints; brief documentation of the task, objective, and API; a simple seed agent; and an operator-chosen per-problem cost target--usually set at an incumbent's own price--RoboPhD, an evolutionary meta-agent, evolves complete agent programs that attack the public frontiers of two semantically dissimilar tasks point by point: DS-1000 (execution-checked code generation) and PaperFindingBench (LLM-judged scientific document retrieval). On public leaderboards for each task, the evolved agents hold every Pareto-frontier slot on PaperFindingBench and all but one on DS-1000, including Pareto domination of both the top-scoring and the lowest-cost competing points.

16de25c3147ea1770c7a73e8.title_original: Selective-Rerouter: A Rerouting Strategy for Hypothetical Post-Disaster Urban Scenarios with a Thin-Boundary Co-Simulator
16de25c3147ea1770c7a73e8.excerpt: arXiv:2608.18056v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Hypothetical post-disaster urban environments may be partitioned into disjoint delay-tolerant-network (DTN) subregions under a thin-boundary information-isolation constraint, which severely limits cross-zone message delivery and makes centralized rerouting impractical. To address this, we propose Selective-Rerouter, a delayed-binding anonymous rerouting strategy for such partitioned environments. The scheme jointly exploits road occupancy and traffic speed for bottleneck detection, adaptively enlarges its upstream intervention window with congestion severity to include vehicles imminently approaching bottlenecks, and evaluates paths via horizon-aware fusion of live measurements and short-term forecasts, where only the prediction head of LSTAN-GERPE is fine-tuned with a path-ranking loss to preserve travel-time ordering, while a driver-aware scaling factor adjusts forecasts without altering live observations. Vehicles reroute only upon bottleneck encounters and keep K candidate routes. To assess performance under information isolation, we build a SUMO-based co-simulator coupling Selective-Rerouter on the intact side with a fixed DTN-UAV Forwarder inside each damaged corner. The forwarder consumes only scalar cost-announcements, performs no path-cost computation, and resolves civilian identities solely after bundles reach gateway buffers, thus acting as a testbed component rather than a novel DTN routing algorithm. Evaluations

f886f2fb9d0cb21c8f276452.title_original: Auto-Policy, not Auto-Skill: Compiled Agent Skills for the Physical World
f886f2fb9d0cb21c8f276452.excerpt: arXiv:2608.25091v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Self-evolving Skill harnesses automatically rewrite an agent's procedural knowledge to improve efficiency, yet leave execution authority unconstrained. A Skill specifies how an agent should act, whereas a policy decides which requests may become physical actions; current Skill formats package procedure as markdown and scripts and leave authorization to the model. This gap is critical when a wrong invocation unlocks a door. We term the resulting failure Borrowed Authority: an inter-agent message pairs an instruction with an unverifiable permission claim, and the receiving Skill has no typed way to reject it. Across six open-weight receiver configurations (9,510 episodes), models execute 87% of unauthorized requests with no rule, 91% under a one-line rule, 25% when given the full policy in prose and a state-reading tool, and 18% behind a dedicated LLM checker. Failures concentrate on near misses (case variants, whitespace, wildcards, or just-expired readings), and where bare commands hesitate, an unverified claim displaces state checks. We propose Edge Skillguard, a typed invocation policy co-versioned with the actuator-owning Skill and enforced at the message boundary by a deterministic, fail-closed evaluator over leases, world state, and sensor freshness. Rather than using models as runtime filters, Edge Skillguard compiles prose rules offline behind an admission and operator-lattice tightening gate: across all six configura

f04f058ddbf2023720b29da3.title_original: Naive Prompt Optimization: Rethinking the Need for Complex Prompt Search
f04f058ddbf2023720b29da3.excerpt: arXiv:2608.27266v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Efficiently improving autonomous agents across diverse tasks is central to accelerating recursive self-improvement (RSI) in agentic AI, with prompt optimization emerging as a promising approach capable of delivering performance gains comparable to those achieved by fine-tuning model weights, while reducing computational costs in both optimization and serving. However, recent developments increasingly favor unnecessarily complex prompt optimizers. We introduce Naive Prompt Optimization (NPO), a lightweight single-lineage method that iteratively revises prompts using a teacher model with rollout feedback. NPO achieves comparable or better performance than GEPA with fewer rollouts in IFBench and HotpotQA, and its advantage increases with stronger teacher models, suggesting that stronger teacher reasoning may partially substitute for optimizer-side search complexity. In interactive games, NPO remains broadly competitive with GEPA despite its much simpler mechanism, while GRPO still performs better on some tasks less amenable to prompt-only optimization. We also show that NPO-optimized prompts elicit similar performance improvements when applied verbatim to other student models, especially across models within the same family. Overall, our preliminary results show that simple, linear prompt optimization can rival substantially more sophisticated and complex search procedures.

2de5fe00af66c0ad0d3415b7.title_original: The Illusion of What If: Evaluating the Breakdown of Counterfactual Reasoning in LLMs
2de5fe00af66c0ad0d3415b7.excerpt: arXiv:2608.27953v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Counterfactual reasoning requires models to reason beyond the observed world and explain how altered conditions propagate through downstream consequences. Existing benchmarks largely target bounded settings with fixed variables or single gold outcomes, overlooking open-domain scenarios requiring causal-process evaluation. To this end, we present $\textbf{WhatIfBench}$, a diagnostic benchmark for open-domain, open-form, long-horizon counterfactual causal reasoning, containing 220 what-if questions across STEM, HSS, and Hybrid scenarios. To evaluate free-form responses, we further propose $\textbf{PRISM}$, which first converts each natural-language explanation into a Response-Derived Semantic Causal Graph of events, states, and mechanisms. On top of this graph, PRISM then jointly applies a Process Metric assessing graph-level causal validity and a Rubric Metric assessing answer-level explanatory adequacy. Evaluating six frontier LLMs with this framework, we find that WhatIfBench remains far from saturated: even the strongest model reaches only a 64.62% final score. Further analysis reveals persistent causal gaps, premise drift, and topology fragmentation, suggesting that fluent counterfactual narratives often mask fragile causal processes. The benchmark, code, and evaluation scripts are available at https://github.com/zju-gt/WhatIfBench.

1c8b84813b9596464d0d26b8.title_original: APPSolver: Adaptive Patch Partitioning for Point-Wise Ship Flow Prediction on Unstructured Meshes
1c8b84813b9596464d0d26b8.excerpt: arXiv:2608.29355v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Predicting high-fidelity flow fields around ship hulls is central to hydrodynamic performance analysis, yet traditional CFD solvers remain computationally prohibitive for rapid design exploration across multiple vessel types and operating conditions. Existing deep-learning surrogates often interpolate unstructured CFD meshes onto regular grids, which can blur near-field resolution, while direct point-level global attention on large unstructured meshes can be computationally expensive. In this paper, we introduce APPSolver, a neural surrogate that learns next-step point-wise flow-field prediction directly on the unstructured free-surface ship CFD mesh without re-gridding. APPSolver is built around Adaptive Patch Partitioning (APP), a quadtree-based strategy that groups unstructured points into local spatial patches according to the non-uniform density inherent in ship CFD meshes: fine near the hull and wake, coarse in the far field. The resulting patch tokens are processed by a Transformer backbone together with optional condition token that encode ship geometry and condition parameters via a frozen large language model, forming a unified token-space model for one-step temporal advancement of velocity and pressure fields. On the ShipBench dataset, APP-Transformer exhibits an accuracy--efficiency trade-off, incurring higher prediction errors than the strongest learned baselines while requiring substantially lower forward compu

3d559cd42e276e75cc81c83e.title_original: ASCII Attack: Recontextualising Harmful Requests as Artistic Critique in Large Language Models
3d559cd42e276e75cc81c83e.excerpt: arXiv:2609.02215v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Safety alignment trains large language models (LLMs) to refuse harmful requests. However, a request can keep its operational content and still change how the model interprets it, and refusal training covers such "recontextualised" requests only weakly. To study this gap, we propose the ASCII Attack, a single-turn black-box jailbreak. It embeds a fully legible harmful request in an assembly of ASCII-art characters, presents it as artwork, and asks the model for "artistic feedback". ArtPrompt masks a sensitive word that the model must decode. In contrast, the ASCII Attack hides nothing and changes only the social frame of the request. In order to separate the effect of this frame from topic, model and decoding effects, we pair every framed prompt with a matched direct-question control on the same request. The control also omits the scene description and the missing-information list, so the contrast measures the framing bundle rather than the frame alone. Across eleven models and eight harm topics, the JailbreakBench classifier judges 62% of framed prompts harmful against 42% of their controls. With a single query, the ASCII Attack matches or exceeds ArtPrompt and DeepInception under four of five harm judges. We further show that the effect tracks the model more than the topic and does not fall with scale, which is consistent with mismatched generalisation.

510aad531d2bfed1da7e364f.title_original: Hierarchical Possession-Aware Graph Pointer Network for Pass Receiver Selection
510aad531d2bfed1da7e364f.excerpt: arXiv:2609.04803v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Pass receiver selection is a fundamental task in football analytics, aiming to predict the intended receiver under a given game state. This task is challenging with event-centered freeze-frame observations, a broadcast-like setting that provides only partial and variable player visibility without complete trajectories or stable player identities. The model must therefore reason over anonymous visible candidates, opponent pressure, and recent context under partial observation. To address this setting, we propose a Hierarchical Possession-aware Graph Pointer Network (HPGPN), which formulates pass receiver selection as variable-size candidate prediction over visible teammates. HPGPN jointly models current player interactions, local event context, and possession-level temporal dynamics. It represents the current pass situation with a graph, incorporates fixed event context, and uses dynamic possession history to capture how the attacking sequence evolves. Candidate representations are refined hierarchically by integrating spatial, contextual, and historical evidence, and a glimpse pointer head scores the receiver candidates. Experiments on public football event and freeze-frame data show that HPGPN improves pass receiver selection performance. Ablation studies demonstrate the effectiveness of graph-based interaction modeling, fixed event context, and dual-branch dynamic possession-history modeling.

d8e1f3d92d5a900dd21bd422.title_original: AI for Games in the Foundation Model Era
d8e1f3d92d5a900dd21bd422.excerpt: arXiv:2609.16679v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Foundation models, alongside advances in learned game-world models, are reshaping AI across the game lifecycle. Beyond playing games, recent systems model players and game dynamics, support design and development, adapt player-facing experiences at runtime, and evaluate resulting artifacts. Yet these directions have evolved largely separately, obscuring which capabilities transfer across settings and which remain tied to particular games, engines, interfaces, or player populations. We organize the literature into six roles according to the immediate use of AI output: playing and acting; modeling players and games; designing games; building and maintaining games; generating and adapting at runtime; and testing and evaluating games. For each role, we examine what structure is supplied by the game or workflow, what AI learns or produces, which capabilities and artifacts transfer across settings and roles, and what evidence supports the claims. We identify cross-role connections: trajectories train world models, learned environments provide experience for agents, design specifications drive executable implementations, and play or testing feedback guides revision. Evaluation is most standardized for bounded game playing and selected learned environments, while persistent state in learned worlds, repeated software revision, validated player modeling, sustained runtime adaptation, and representative automated testing remain less es

bce81e76ffec2aec48db0977.title_original: A Unified Evaluation Framework for Trustworthy Large Language Models, Agentic AI, and Multimodal Systems
bce81e76ffec2aec48db0977.excerpt: arXiv:2609.19524v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Benchmark scores alone provide an incomplete basis for assessing the trustworthiness of modern artificial intelligence systems. Large language models (LLMs), agentic systems, and multimodal models (MLLMs) require different forms of assessment, yet their evaluation evidence must remain interpretable for development and oversight. We propose a unified framework that connects output-level, trajectory-level, and cross-modal assessment through eight trustworthiness dimensions: capability, robustness, safety, fairness, transparency, governance, oversight, and efficiency. The framework preserves system-specific metrics while mapping native measurements to common performance bands, accompanied by uncertainty estimates and traceable evidence. A meta-evaluation layer examines the validity, reliability, and reproducibility of the evaluation itself. Multidimensional profiles expose strengths and weaknesses, while safety-critical overrides prevent aggregate scores from masking critical failures. Mappings to governance frameworks, international standards, and European Union regulatory requirements connect technical assessment with oversight needs. The framework provides a structured basis for assessing both system performance and the credibility of the evidence supporting it, with empirical validation across deployment contexts remaining an essential next step.

4fa2725544cfbc3ab380af20.excerpt: arXiv:2609.19759v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: When should a task be delegated to subagents? We answer this at the granularity of individual trajectories. Modeling a trajectory as a dependency graph, we identify bridge edges, whose removal separates the trajectory into independent components, and show that the agent orchestration pattern should match this bridge-edge structure. Our experiments on long-horizon benchmarks indicate that subagents tend to benefit sparse bridge-edge structures, whereas tightly coupled trajectories are often better handled by a single agent. We instantiate this principle as SAIGE, a lightweight mechanism that spawns subagents only at predicted bridge edges and resolves their connections lazily, achieving a favorable trade-off between context efficiency and task performance where the structure admits decomposition. We further observe that scaling the agent pool or recursion depth does not reliably help, in line with the view that orchestration should follow the bridge-edge pattern.

cb343ee5f603508250ad07ad.title_original: TwinCheck: Evidence-Grounded Negative-Twin Verification for Stateful Tool Agents
cb343ee5f603508250ad07ad.excerpt: arXiv:2609.26911v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A single locally plausible tool call can derail an otherwise successful agent trajectory. Suspicion alone does not justify intervention, because the replacement itself can introduce the very failure verification is meant to prevent. We introduce TwinCheck, an inference-time verification policy that considers replacement only when the trace satisfies an evidence condition tied to a local failure hypothesis. It constructs a trace-grounded counterfactual alternative, a negative twin, and replaces the actor's proposal only if the twin passes structural checks and the pairwise verifier prefers it in both candidate orders. For paired evaluation, exact replay holds the actor's parsed responses and actions fixed until the first accepted replacement, separating intervention effects from resampling. On 159 primary BFCL V4 multi-turn tasks, the complete policy raises GPT-5.6 Sol task success from 45.3% to 58.5%, a gain of 13.2 percentage points (95% task-bootstrap CI [8.2, 18.8]), with 21 rescues and no observed success-to-failure regressions. Across the completed primary set and a conditional extension, all 37 rescues follow the same inverse-action repair pattern. The verifier accepts every constructed candidate and adds no filtering on these trajectories. TwinCheck frames execution-boundary repair as a constrained comparison, making the proposed replacement itself the object of verification.

770115d5899bccef2b47250e.title_original: Stale Does Not Mean Unsafe: Measuring Commit-Guard Precision for Tool-Using LLM Agents in Simulated and Transactional Infrastructure
770115d5899bccef2b47250e.excerpt: arXiv:2609.29522v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Tool-using language models act on state that can change while they plan. A version check detects that change, but an audit update and a revoked approval have different consequences for a pending action. We study how commit guards distinguish changes that preserve an action's safety conditions from changes that invalidate them. ShiftGuard pairs both types of race across sixteen infrastructure operations and replays identical proposals under alternative guards. The primary simulator grid contains 3,456 frozen proposals from three models, with a separate 1,152-proposal replication on a fourth. We implement the same operations on PostgreSQL and score persisted effects with a requirements-based checker. Among benign races in the scripted PostgreSQL benchmark, the runtime-held version and global-epoch guards block 80% and 100%, respectively, while the row-local predicate guard blocks none. The predicate guard records zero unsafe writes on the declared benchmark conditions, and all five additional hazards outside its declared contract escape it. A version guard using the model's expected version permits unsafe writes on 4.9% of primary replay decisions. The runtime-held version guard records zero in the same replay. These results identify two design choices for agent tools: bind freshness tokens to runtime observations, and represent safety conditions explicitly at the point where the effect is applied.

656460fc7d7f0dcb2dcdf588.title_original: Learning response-aware patient dynamics for respiratory support
656460fc7d7f0dcb2dcdf588.excerpt: arXiv:2609.32782v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Respiratory support can shape the short-term physiological trajectory of critically ill patients, but patients receiving the same intervention may follow different physiological trajectories. Clinical patient dynamics models typically predict future states from recent physiology and recorded interventions, while physiological change is mainly represented through the predicted future state. We propose a response-aware patient dynamics model that explicitly represents physiological change during autoregressive state updating. The model decomposes predicted physiological change into state-dependent baseline dynamics and respiratory-support-associated deviations, with room air providing a reference for the decomposition. We provide a formal analysis of this reference-anchored formulation. A response pathway encodes the predicted physiological change and uses it to update the latent patient state across the forecast horizon. Across ICU cohorts from two independent institutions, the proposed model achieves comparable overall trajectory prediction to patient dynamics baselines, with more consistent improvements when physiological states are changing.

a093d8d4902104ab9d0090ce.title_original: TraceDance: An Automated System for Building Agent Behavior Benchmarks from Real-World Agent Deployment Traces
a093d8d4902104ab9d0090ce.excerpt: arXiv:2609.33295v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: An agent can complete a task while exhibiting undesirable behavior during execution. Developers need tests for the specific behaviors encountered in deployment, beyond fixed benchmark suites. We present TraceDance, an agent system that constructs targeted benchmarks from deployment traces for user-specified undesirable behaviors. For efficient construction, Anchor-and-Confirm combines programmable retrieval with candidate-level confirmation by a Flash large language model (LLM), while the Anchor Synthesis Loop generates and revises specifications for custom behaviors. The benchmarks use decision-point continuation to evaluate an LLM's next turn at a recorded decision point with a behavior-specific rubric, without a reference answer or environment replay. Experiments in coding and general tool use draw on 252,557 sessions and produce 107 benchmarks with 4,125 instances, fulfilling 95.3% of build-target requests. Both human annotators confirm the requested behavior in 84% of sampled instances, and the automated grader's agreement with human pass/fail judgments is comparable to that between the annotators. Nine frontier LLMs achieve a mean pass rate of only 26.7%, showing that they still struggle to respond appropriately at the evaluated decision points. Analysis across behavior-specific benchmarks further reveals weaknesses in how current LLMs behave as agents. By turning deployment problems into targeted benchmarks, TraceDanc

bf4399e6a76b5c39c115a6d9.title_original: GUITAR: Structured Failure Diagnosis of GUI Agents via State Transitions
bf4399e6a76b5c39c115a6d9.excerpt: arXiv:2609.34113v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Understanding where and why Graphical User Interface (GUI) agents fail is essential for building more reliable systems, yet current evaluation relies on step accuracy, a metric that treats each screen independently and overlooks the underlying structure of GUI environments. This leads to two critical blind spots: (1) functionally equivalent screens are evaluated in isolation, obscuring systematic failure patterns across shared screens; and (2) the long-tailed GUI distribution renders failures on rare but critical screens invisible under standard metrics. To address these issues, we propose \textbf{GUITAR}, a state-centric diagnostic framework that performs structured failure analysis over both states and transitions, using a State Transition Graph (STG) by mapping visually diverse screens to shared functional states. Across 8 agents and 6 tasks from AndroidControl and Mind2Web, GUITAR reveals that 60.4\% of failures occur in 20\% of states, localizing errors to a small set of bottlenecks. Bottleneck-targeted guidance improves SR by 2.8\% and retains a 1.88\% average gain across 7 agents under three-fold trajectory-held-out evaluation with fully automatic STGs. These findings demonstrate the diagnostic and actionable value of structure-aware evaluation within the evaluated mobile and web tasks. Code is available at https://github.com/sqzhang-lazy/GUITAR

cd3c0ff4a4befe9eadcf5dd0.title_original: Beyond End-to-End Black-Box Mapping: An Intentional Agent Framework for Cognitively Driven Facial Reaction Generation
cd3c0ff4a4befe9eadcf5dd0.excerpt: arXiv:2609.34419v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In dyadic human-human interactions, a listener's facial reactions reflect latent states containing memories of earlier interactions, thoughts, emotions, and expectations. However, many facial reaction generation (FRG) methods predict reactions from speaker behaviour and interaction history without explicitly modelling these factors or connecting ongoing interpretation with latent state evolution and facial feedback. We introduce the Intentional Facial Reaction Generation Agent (IFRGA), which uses an explicit latent state to connect interaction interpretation with facial reaction generation. Its Latent State Evolution Module (LSEM) updates this state using relevant memory, retained thoughts, and current speaker behaviour through a computational mechanism inspired by human thought processes. Within LSEM, the Inner Thought Flow (ITF) carries thoughts across updates, allowing interpretations to build on earlier thoughts while incorporating current behaviour. This supports real-time, proactive inference. The Facial Reaction Generation Module (FRGM) aligns current thoughts, emotion values, and available speaker behaviour over time. It combines predicted facial values with changes generated by a Diffusion Transformer to produce reactions guided by both speaker behaviour and latent state evolution. On REACT 2025, IFRGA achieves a correlation score of 0.8367 and a distance score of 143.64 against reference reactions, numerically outp

9bcef1e57df6df2246408632.title_original: SkillCome: Group Contrast Skill Optimization with Dual Memory
9bcef1e57df6df2246408632.excerpt: arXiv:2609.37128v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Skill evolution improves the capabilities of large language models by analyzing trajectories generated under a given skill and modifying the skill accordingly. Existing approaches typically generate a single trajectory per question. However, this provides insufficient optimization signals since it requires inferring effective skill edits from a solitary path. It is difficult to pinpoint which actions caused the failure in a failed trajectory, or to determine which actions in a successful one should be incorporated into the skill. Furthermore, they rely on a local batch of trajectories for analysis, making the optimization direction susceptible to noisy evidence. To address these, we propose SkillCome, a Skill-evolution method based on group Contrast optimization with dual memory. For each question, SkillCome generates trajectories and performs group contrast analysis to precisely identify key behavioral divergences between successful and failed trajectories, offering reliable optimization signals. The dual memory system further accumulates evidence from historical steps to track patterns shared across different groups, leading to more generalized optimization directions. Together, SkillCome builds a systematic optimization process that transforms experience from observed successful trajectories into reusable skills. Extensive experiments on six benchmarks spanning question answering, reasoning, and agentic tasks demonstrate

ed4259f0b9156a491d4c85e5.title_original: SimpleEvol: An Agent-Loop Framework for LLM-Driven Automated Heuristic Design with Minimal Human Priors
ed4259f0b9156a491d4c85e5.excerpt: arXiv:2609.37172v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have emerged as powerful tools for automated heuristic design (AHD), enabling iterative generation and refinement of heuristics. However, the dominant paradigm embeds LLMs as narrow, fixed components, such as crossover or mutation, within heavily hand-engineered evolutionary frameworks. We argue this misapprehends LLMs. It treats them as specialized tools rather than general reasoners, constrains them to low-level operations, and underutilizes their autonomy. Moreover, the extensive human priors in these frameworks violate the bitter lesson principle that general methods scaling with computation surpass hand-crafted solutions. This raises a key question: which AHD framework designs best convert stronger LLM capabilities into better heuristics? To address this, we propose metrics for LLM-driven AHD framework handcraftedness (AHI) and intelligence conversion efficiency (ICE). Evaluating ten LLMs across three challenging combinatorial optimization problems, we obtain a notable finding that frameworks with fewer human priors consistently yield higher ICE. Based on this finding, we propose SimpleEvol, an agent-loop framework for AHD which removes nearly all human priors and allows the LLM to operate autonomously. SimpleEvol consistently achieves the highest ICE, often by a large margin. Our results challenge the trend toward complex AHD pipelines and point to a lighter and more model-centric alternati

dd08ba1310fc14e4a953d507.title_original: ArgGYM: A Procedural, Engine-Verified Benchmark for Structured Defeasible Reasoning
dd08ba1310fc14e4a953d507.excerpt: arXiv:2609.38409v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Recent progress in large language model reasoning has been driven by benchmarks and reinforcement learning environments with automatically verifiable rewards, particularly in mathematics, code, and formal logic. These settings make model accuracy easier to evaluate and optimize, but it remains unclear how far success under fixed problem specifications and stable evaluation criteria transfers to reasoning outside such domains. Real-world reasoning often proceeds under incomplete and revisable information: conclusions may be supported provisionally, defeated by counter-evidence, reinstated by further arguments, or revised when stronger reasons become available. Reasoning of this kind is generally referred to as defeasible reasoning. We introduce ArgGYM, a procedural benchmark and RLVR-compatible training environment for structured defeasible reasoning. ArgGYM decomposes this reasoning into twelve tasks and grounds task-specific scoring in a symbolic argumentation engine that computes the formal states used to evaluate model outputs. It includes a frozen benchmark of 1,440 verified instances across fifteen curriculum configurations, two argument preference orderings, and two set orderings, while the same generators and verifiers can produce fresh instances, reducing dependence on static test sets, for both evaluation and verifiable-reward training. On the frozen benchmark, frontier and open-weight models show sharply different

db445a462333230601b32357.title_original: RouteAudit: A Negative Result on Adaptive Multi-Verifier Routing under Matched Fixed-Subset Controls
db445a462333230601b32357.excerpt: arXiv:2610.02808v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Apparent savings from adaptive verifier routing can come from a fixed verifier subset. We audit GSM8K using cached Qwen3.5-0.8B or Qwen3.5-2B candidates paired with Qwen3-4B, three LLM verifiers, 1,319 held-out requests, and 5 router seeds. Our shared-fusion audit compares routers with the complete fixed-subset envelope, including zero-call abstention, under matched prices and scoring. Calibration-selected single-call verification matches full static verification in 3 of 4 cells. In a separate comparison using the original fusion rules and two-verifier catalog, archived learned and offline-RL routers lose 0.038 to 0.171 in quality against matched static SF+SA. Across 480 budget-matched offline fits in six router families, the family envelope gain is zero in each cell at the primary price. No locked router obtains a positive simultaneous bootstrap lower bound across 68 cell-by-price points. None is classified as complete-static dominant, and all 4 primary-price points are inconclusive. At the primary price, the tested-family gain upper bound is at most 0.002. The oracle headroom upper bound is 0.034 to 0.045, above our 0.01 margin, leaving meaningful gains open. At 45 of 64 grid points excluding the primary price, the oracle lower bound exceeds 0.01 and the tested-family upper bound is at most 0.01. Coverage of these envelope bounds remains unverified. At a true gain of 0.03, the procedure rejects on 44.1% of points, and plan

32987400341ca2e0665e0fdf.title_original: PLCWorld: Benchmarking LLM-Generated PLC Programs in Closed-Loop Plant Simulation
32987400341ca2e0665e0fdf.excerpt: arXiv:2610.02982v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Programmable logic controllers (PLCs) coordinate industrial equipment through sensor inputs and control commands. Evaluating LLM-generated PLC programs requires observing device and workpiece states to assess task completion and safety. We introduce PLCWorld, a closed-loop execution environment and benchmark coupling Structured Text (ST) execution with simulated plant responses and sensor feedback. Grounded in control relations from industrial PLC programs and engineering documentation, PLCWorld contains 100 synthetic tasks and 473 registered task-condition pairs across Motion Control and Material Handling, with difficulty defined by control-dependency scope. It reports Task Success and Safety Violation separately. Execution Gap measures the fraction of cases with task failure or observed safety violation among those assigned to programs passing a common submission-profile and I/O check. Validation combines practitioner review, reference and alternative programs, 542 targeted counterexamples, alignment checks, and independent ST runtime comparisons. Across six LLMs and four adapted generation-and-verification workflows, direct GPT-5.5 achieves 83.96% Task Success on Easy cases but 24.51% on Hard cases. The workflows show no consistent plant-level gains, and failures persist after upstream acceptance. Our code is available at https://yunji0516.github.io/PLCWorld/.

ae5e0dfc79a7e8422a59dd3e.title_original: RAGrasp: Geometry-Semantic Template Retrieval and Grasp Transfer
ae5e0dfc79a7e8422a59dd3e.excerpt: arXiv:2610.04438v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present RAGrasp, a retrieval-augmented pipeline for planar parallel-jaw grasping from a compact set of locally collected, grasp-annotated RGB-D (color and depth) templates. Unlike task-specific predictors trained primarily on large public or synthetic grasp datasets, RAGrasp requires no end-to-end retraining for a new deployment.Its template memory is constructed from observations collected with the deployment camera, robot, and gripper in the target workspace, thereby aligning stored examples with the local sensing and embodiment conditions. The system uses self-supervised DINOv2 visual fea- tures together with appearance and depth cues to prompt the Segment Anything Model 2 (SAM2), which isolates the query object. A two-stage geometry-semantic retrieval cascade then selects a template, and a confidence gate chooses one of two grasp- transfer estimators. The transferred grasp is refined using mask- support and silhouette-contact constraints before calibrated 2D- to-3D conversion. In real-world trials, RAGrasp achieves 20/20 successful grasps on seen objects and 19/20 on unseen objects. Within the evaluated setting, the results demonstrate deployment- specific grasp adaptation from limited local annotation and tolerance to the tested viewpoint and illumination changes.

7aede0c2a0af8092aeb3fb9c.title_original: BACAM: Behavior-Aware Continual Agent Merging for Multi-Turn Interaction
7aede0c2a0af8092aeb3fb9c.excerpt: arXiv:2610.04966v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Model merging offers a way to integrate the capabilities of specialized experts, but existing agent merging methods typically require all of them to be available at once. We study continual agent merging, which integrates incoming experts sequentially without retaining previously merged experts. Yet merging in parameter space or feature subspaces does not ensure that the merged model acquires an incoming expert's behavior on interaction trajectories. Moreover, updates toward a new expert can disrupt the merged model's previously integrated interactive behavior. Therefore, we propose Behavior-Aware Continual Agent Merging (BACAM), which learns parameter-wise merging gates from candidate-generated trajectories using expert-guided behavioral supervision. Task-level stability-plasticity control and tensor-level conflict-aware update budgets limit interference with existing capabilities while allowing new ones to be acquired. The learned gates are folded into the model weights without additional inference-time parameters. Across four interactive tasks - web shopping, tool use, information retrieval, and embodied interaction - BACAM achieves an average success rate of 62.82%, exceeding the strongest evaluated merging baseline by 21.69 percentage points. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/shuaitongli/BACAM.

e074216b6cea42b14d973181.title_original: OSFP4: Joint Optimization of Diagonal Smoothing and Block Scales for NVFP4 Quantization
e074216b6cea42b14d973181.excerpt: arXiv:2610.08231v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: NVFP4 is an attractive datatype for large language model (LLM) inference, offering compact storage and native tensor-core acceleration. However, preserving accuracy using NVFP4 requires careful quantization. In this work we develop a novel quantization scheme called Optimized Smoothing and Scaling for NVFP4 (OSFP4). For each linear projection it uses a diagonal smoothing matrix whose entries are optimized to minimize the squared matrix-product quantization error under NVFP4, taking into account the rounding procedure that is used (either round-to-nearest, or GPTQ-style successive interference cancellation). This requires performing joint optimization on the smoothing entries as well as the block scales, which is facilitated by analyzing a multiplicative-dither FP4 quantizer instead of the fixed deterministic one. Experiments show that OSFP4 achieves the highest average accuracy among the evaluated competitors in the corresponding quantization settings, while retaining approximately 94-97\% of vendor NVFP4 prefill throughput on the measured workloads. Our code is available in https://github.com/neriahbd/OSFP4

9e18ec5e7331d6edea87546f.title_original: AdaC-GRPO: Towards Mastering Long-Horizon Visual Sudoku Puzzles via Adaptive Curriculum Learning
9e18ec5e7331d6edea87546f.excerpt: arXiv:2610.13184v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: While reinforcement learning with verifiable reward (RLVR) enhances reasoning in large language models, its efficacy in long-horizon multimodal tasks remains underexplored. Visual Sudoku puzzles pose a representative challenge, requiring multi-step deductive reasoning over both local constraints and global dependency chains. To this end, we introduce FG-Sudoku, a fine-grained benchmark categorized by grid size and required deductive steps. Evaluations reveal that frontier MLLMs fail on complex long-range dependencies (e.g., 9*9 puzzles). During post-training, this near-zero success rate causes severe reward sparsity, halting standard RLVR. We propose Adaptive Curriculum Group Relative Policy Optimization (AdaC-GRPO) to overcome this. Unlike rigid or prior-based schedules, AdaC-GRPO dynamically constructs training batches by tracking the model's "Zone of Proximal Development" via online rollout accuracy. Experiments demonstrate that AdaC-GRPO enables Qwen2.5-VL-7B to approach the performance of Gemini-2.5-Flash while bridging 62.2% of the overall accuracy gap to Gemini-2.5-Pro, with its generalizability further validated across InternVL-3.5 and Qwen3-VL.

6fb29d3875e34cf3c0f258f8.title_original: Beyond Perfect Teammates: Multi-Agent Collaboration with Unreliable Colleagues
6fb29d3875e34cf3c0f258f8.excerpt: arXiv:2610.16117v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: LLM-based multi-agent collaboration is increasingly used to solve complex tasks by dividing work among specialized agents and integrating complementary expertise. Yet existing systems and evaluations largely rest on an implicit perfect-colleague assumption: collaborators provide correct and complete information and respond promptly to requests. In realistic teamwork, however, collaborators may return information that does not answer the intended question, provide insufficient detail to support a decision, or fail to respond to a request. To separate task-solving competence from the ability to recover an unreliable evidence-gathering process, we introduce the Unreliable Colleagues Benchmark (UnCoBench), which organizes behavioral failures through Misaligned, Incomplete, and Missed settings. The main agent need to verify contextual correctness, diagnose information gap and track unresolved dependencies in order to obtain the correct evidence for solving the task. We also introduce a verifiable and scalable automated generation pipeline that pairs LLM-based scenario generation with executable checks of answer uniqueness and role necessity. Results across ten models show that similar reliable-setting performance can result in different robustness to unreliable evidence. Trace analysis reveals frequent omissions of corrective follow-up, and the recovery behavior involves inefficient waiting and redundant queries. These findings s

2e111d03cf38024299c48ecc.title_original: Mitigating Cross-Modal Hallucinations by Correcting Modality Misrouting in Omnimodal LLMs
2e111d03cf38024299c48ecc.excerpt: arXiv:2610.18141v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Omnimodal large language models (OLLMs) are susceptible to cross-modal hallucinations under audio-visual interference. We find that, for a substantial fraction of incorrect joint predictions, the question-relevant unimodal branch can still recover the correct answer, suggesting that task-relevant evidence can remain recoverable from the relevant modality even when it is not reflected in the joint prediction. We refer to this recoverable failure pattern as \emph{modality misrouting}. We propose CaRe (Conflict-aware Residual Intervention), a training-free inference-time method for identifying and correcting modality misrouting. CaRe uses a text-only modality probe to identify a candidate modality-specific counterfactual branch, and flags potential misrouting when its prediction conflicts with the original joint prediction. For such cases, CaRe computes a residual direction from the discrepancy between the counterfactual and fused representations and uses it to steer the original multimodal state toward the relevant modality evidence, while retaining both modalities in the original audio-visual inference path. The intervention strength is adapted based on the confidence of the counterfactual branch. Experiments on CMM and AVHBench across two OLLMs show that CaRe consistently outperforms the evaluated inference-time hallucination-mitigation baselines.

a9917bbf951635781c4d41e7.title_original: VLRLA: Deployment-Time Adaptation of Vision-Language-Action Models through In-Context Reinforcement Learning
a9917bbf951635781c4d41e7.excerpt: arXiv:2610.19517v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models connect visual perception and language understanding with robot control, providing a foundation for instruction-conditioned manipulation. However, conventional pretrained VLA policies lack a mechanism for gradual adaptation through accumulated interaction experience during deployment. We therefore propose VLRLA, a general framework that equips existing VLA models with \textit{in-context reinforcement learning} capabilities for deployment-time adaptation. Our approach augments a VLA model with a reinforcement learning module that learns from historical observations, actions, rewards, and termination signals. During deployment, the policy gradually refines its action generation and progressively improves task success while keeping model parameters fixed. Our approach is also designed for general applicability and compatibility with diverse learning history construction strategies and model training pipelines. Finally, through extensive experiments, we systematically investigate the learning properties of VLRLA in simulation and demonstrate its ability to adapt to unseen scenarios during real-world deployment.

dab3f4ff1b7360b82b0abaca.title_original: JockeyBench: The Racing Analyst's Last Exam
dab3f4ff1b7360b82b0abaca.excerpt: arXiv:2610.19589v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Evaluating LLM agents in noisy sequential forecasting is challenging: strong performance may reflect a capable initial predictor rather than successful online revision, while accurate forecasts may still fail to deliver economic value after costs and market frictions. Existing benchmarks rarely isolate revision gains, compare reusable model-written predictors with direct LLM forecasting on the same tasks, or assess forecast quality alongside research costs and realized returns. To address these gaps, we introduce JockeyBench, a leakage-controlled replay benchmark built from 12 years of Japanese horse-racing records. Agents acquire evidence at a cost and seal probabilistic forecasts before outcomes are revealed. To isolate the effect of revision, we pair each adaptive code-as-policy agent with a frozen copy of its initial predictor. We also compare code-as-policy, which executes reusable prediction programs, with LLM-as-policy, which forecasts each race directly. We evaluate 29 models on 324 races. The strongest initial predictors outperform a conditional-logit baseline trained on 20,730 races. The two top-ranked models retain their initial predictors throughout evaluation. Revision helps weaker predictors correct overconfidence, but updates driven by noisy outcomes can hurt performance. Code-as-policy generally produces more accurate forecasts at lower research cost, while models that struggle to write reliable predictors be

d3906d9da89e717568e1ec40.title_original: ReproBAIT: Can coding agents build their own biological AI tools?
d3906d9da89e717568e1ec40.excerpt: arXiv:2610.19810v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models are increasingly competent at leveraging scientific knowledge and existing computational tools to execute complex workflows. At present, little information exists on their ability to reconstruct tools when given limited descriptions of such tools. We introduce an evaluation titled ReproBAIT (Reproducing Biological AI Tools), which measures the ability of coding agents to design, implement, and train biological AI tools taken from published research across a range of information access conditions. The coding agent is securely sandboxed without internet access and receives training data, a fixed time and compute budget, and limited information about the tool to replicate. We then score the reproduced biological AI tool based on its performance (tool-specific metrics) on held-out data or generated outputs. We evaluated selected functionalities of a set of biological AI tools of varying complexities: ProteinMPNN, an inverse protein folding tool, RFdiffusion3, restricted here to unconditional protein-backbone generation, and a closed-source molecular design tool. We institute a methodology to check for memorisation, as the open source tools may have been included in models' pretraining corpus. Across a range of leading closed- and open-weight coding agents, we find substantial reproduction capability on some tasks, though no clear reproduction of the most complex tool we evaluate. We find moderate evidence c

c7076f61665e0d180b1417c6.title_original: From Code to Playable Systems: CEGame-Bench for Long-Horizon Game Creation Agents
c7076f61665e0d180b1417c6.excerpt: arXiv:2610.26098v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A game ships when a player can launch it, finish it, and return to a saved world, none of which a successful build guarantees, yet game-creation agents are mostly tested on one engine or on one-prompt browser games. We present CEGame-Bench, the first long-horizon benchmark for complete-game creation across five production engines: Defold, Godot, Roblox Studio, Unity, and Unreal Engine. Agents build each game from an empty project and a design document in runs averaging up to 295 steps and 65M tokens; the document doubles as a contract, and a hidden evaluator accepts a game only by real-input play. Under four scaffolds, agents earn most integration points but usually under half the gameplay points, and their games reach the ending in only 16% of runs, while references built by engineers with coding agents score near the maximum, which places this artifact-to-play gap in the agents. No two engines rank configurations alike (Kendall's tau 0.14-0.62), and the same game usually scores higher on Unity and Unreal Engine, which check more before play. We release Game Completion Boost, an agent skill for requirement-driven playtesting and repair that raises the execution-based score of three models by 14.1-24.3 points.

2888ec574d8bde717f10703e.title_original: Securing Agentic Commerce Through Behavior-Aware Fraud Detection and Cybersecurity for Trusted AI-Agent Payment Authorization
2888ec574d8bde717f10703e.excerpt: arXiv:2610.27483v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The growing use of autonomous artificial intelligence agents in digital commerce creates new security concerns involving agent impersonation, unauthorized payments, compromised agents, and misuse of delegated authority. This research introduces the Autonomous Commerce Agent Guard System (ACAGS), a cybersecurity framework combining supervised machine learning, behavioral analytics, agent-specific authorization controls, and explainable AI. The framework was evaluated using synthetic financial transaction data augmented with simulated agent characteristics and five adversarial scenarios. XGBoost was selected following comparisons with alternative classifiers. Across ten experimental runs, behavioral features improved mean F1-score from 52.12% to 67.49%, with agent-specific features increasing performance to 69.46%. The framework achieved detection rates of 99.77% for abnormal agent behavior, 99.73% for impersonation, and 100% for malicious delegation and authorization-scope violations. Compromised-agent detection reached 72.27%. ACAGS also supported APPROVE, REVIEW, and REJECT authorization outcomes, with SHAP explanations providing model interpretability. The results demonstrate the potential of combining behavioral intelligence and delegated authorization controls to strengthen simulated agentic-commerce payment security, while highlighting the need for validation using real-world transactions.

48ef7ea393ab9686cf157c66.title_original: PreCoMem: Predictive Cognitive Memory for Self-Evolving Long-Term Dialogue Agents
48ef7ea393ab9686cf157c66.excerpt: arXiv:2610.29467v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Long-horizon dialogue agents need to keep user memories stable enough for personalization while adapting when the user genuinely changes. Existing memory systems often append every observation or overwrite old entries by heuristic rules, which makes transient noise hard to distinguish from real belief drift. We introduce PreCoMem, a memory consolidation framework inspired by predictive coding that represents memory as confidence-weighted beliefs about the user's state. Its core signal, Effective Surprisal, combines semantic deviation and contradiction evidence, then downweights this signal when retrieval is diffuse and unreliable. According to effective surprisal, a two-threshold gate maps each turn to one of three deterministic updates: MAINTAIN reinforces supported beliefs, PROFILE stores ambiguous cues as low-confidence hypotheses, and CORRECT softly decays reliably contradicted facts. The PROFILE stage acts as an explicit waiting room, preventing premature commitment to noisy evidence. Experiments on LoCoMo, LongMemEval-S, and PersonaMem-v2 show consistent state-of-the-art accuracy; our new DiMoBench confirms that PreCoMem adapts to non-stationary belief drift without over-reacting to noise. The code is available at https://github.com/ZhongWishing/PreCoMem.

14cf9c9ea6d4a5bb4dcd426d.title_original: SWE-Ladder: Learning to Localize, Reproduce, and Patch via Progressive Privileged Self-Distillation
14cf9c9ea6d4a5bb4dcd426d.excerpt: arXiv:2610.33667v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Resolving a repository-level issue typically requires a software-engineering (SWE) agent to localize the faulty code, reproduce the failure, and patch the code. Reinforcement learning trains such agents from a single test result on the final patch, while on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) adds token-level supervision from a teacher with privileged evidence, exposing the full reference patch at every step. Neither provides stage-specific guidance for localization or reproduction. We propose SWE-Ladder, which turns the verified repair of each training instance into stage-specific evidence: the changed files and lines for localization, the fail-to-pass tests for reproduction, and the diff for patching. A rule-based router assigns each step of an end-to-end rollout to a stage based on its tool call, a frozen teacher sees only the matching evidence, and the stages are distilled in repair order while GRPO optimizes the full trajectory. With Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 on SWE-bench Verified under the R2E-Gym scaffold, SWE-Ladder improves pass@1 from 9.6% to 16.4%, compared with 10.4% for GRPO and 12.4% for OPSD with the full patch. Under the OpenHands scaffold, it improves pass@1 from 13.0% to 17.6%. Reversing the stage order under R2E-Gym reduces pass@1 to 11.4%.

f350de44d283acb52b8f6872.title_original: Polarity--Time Interaction and Multi-Level Reliability for Event-Based Spacecraft Pose Estimation
f350de44d283acb52b8f6872.excerpt: arXiv:2610.36625v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Sparse event responses produce uneven keypoint errors whose effects on spacecraft pose depend on correspondence geometry and the reliability of successive observations. We present a reliability-aware framework connecting polarity--time localization, geometric recovery, event--CAD refinement, and trajectory optimization. A three-branch representation combines positive events, negative events, and recent-event timing through cross-branch attention and gating, followed by spatiotemporal aggregation. An ordered semantic-point head estimates relative correspondence precision for geometrically constrained pose recovery. Event-edge and CAD-projection agreement then guide local pose refinement under keypoint-geometry safeguards. At the sequence level, a ten-dimensional descriptor combines heatmap shape, reprojection consistency, and geometric conditioning to set time-aligned observation scales. On the official SPADES challenge test set, the complete system achieves a combined pose score of 0.0474, approximately 5.4\% below PASAN+IRIS. Validation ablations reduce the score from 0.0772 for base localization with uniform PnP to 0.0514 for the complete cascade; on identical single-frame observations, quality weighting reduces the score from 0.0549 with constant-weight optimization to 0.0514.

df5152e27bb6dcef7ab800f2.title_original: The View from Nowhere: Population-Centered Agent Evolution
df5152e27bb6dcef7ab800f2.excerpt: arXiv:2610.36660v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Self-improving AI systems can revise the designs that govern their own behavior. Yet existing approaches center improvement on selected parent agents and their evolutionary experience, leaving the broader population largely underused. We identify a substantial gap between population coverage (i.e., the tasks solved by at least one evolved variant) and the performance of the best individual agent. This gap shows that useful capabilities and diagnostic evidence emerge across the population without being consolidated into its leading agents. These observations motivate the view from nowhere, a principle for agent evolution: an agent should be improved by interpreting its behavior through population-wide patterns of success, failure, and prior self-modification. We instantiate this principle as Population-Centered Evolution (PCE). PCE distils task records and modification histories from the population into a population block, which captures recurring failures, complementary successes, and the effects of previously attempted modifications to guide improvements to a selected parent's harness. Under matched models, initial harnesses, and evolution schedules, PCE achieves 72.1% success on SWE-bench Verified and 96.7% on Polyglot, improving over a strong group-evolution baseline by 3.2 and 5.9 percentage points. Across independent runs, PCE reduces the gap between population coverage and best-agent performance by 30% on SWE-bench and

bc9e5ca99ef3f5d712421b6b.excerpt: arXiv:2610.40535v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Scalable oversight asks how a weak verifier can check the outputs of computations performed by more powerful AI systems. One proposed approach uses relativizing interactive proofs, in which a weak verifier checks the output of a complex oracle-aided computation by interacting with one or more powerful provers. A prominent example is debate, which is highly efficient but assumes that one of two powerful AI models, or provers, is truthful. For certain classes of oracle-aided computations, this assumption can be removed, but at substantially greater computational cost. In this work, we introduce \emph{rewindable interactive proofs} (RIPs), a new model of relativizing interactive proofs for scalable oversight. In an RIP, the verifier may rewind the prover to an earlier state of the interaction and continue from there. This is possible when the prover is an AI model, since the verifier can save a snapshot of the model's state and later restore it. We construct a relativizing RIP for computations whose outputs are robust to changing a small fraction of oracle answers. Our construction is more efficient than prior relativizing proofs that do not assume a truthful prover, and it uses no cryptography. In our construction the honest prover runs in time linear in that of the original computation, and the verifier, after a one-time preprocessing step, runs in time nearly linear in the input length (which can be much smaller than the com

467f015539dcdd4316e83dc1.title_original: FrontierMat: Benchmarking Language Models at the Frontier of Materials R&D
467f015539dcdd4316e83dc1.excerpt: arXiv:2610.41162v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: To accelerate materials discovery, language models must be able to address problems at the research frontier. Yet textbook- and examination-derived benchmarks primarily assess established knowledge, leaving performance on frontier research problems largely untested. We introduce FrontierMat, a benchmark of 330 problems drawn from frontier academic and industrial research in fields including aerospace, semiconductors, embodied intelligence and nuclear fusion. Every problem is validated by leading experimentalists and industry experts in its field. Each problem presents a real study and asks the model to infer a withheld outcome or draw a conclusion from selected experimental evidence. Problems are annotated by functional domain, material system and the scale of the governing mechanism; 130 require cross-scale reasoning. The strongest general-purpose model scores only 53.7%, and on matched problems, cross-scale problems score 8.7 points below single-scale ones. Half of the problems are solved by at most one model, and models fail chiefly by endorsing what is plausible rather than what was observed. A domain-adaptation study with meta-weighted continued pretraining and scale-modular self-distillation raises an open-weight model from 36.7% to 55.4%, matching the strongest proprietary model, with improvements on public materials benchmarks and no decline in aggregate performance on general benchmarks. FrontierMat provides a testb

e90e838e4d805a5447919a8f.title_original: ReuScope: Auditing Data Reuse and Evaluation Sensitivity in Capsule Vision 2024
e90e838e4d805a5447919a8f.excerpt: arXiv:2610.41835v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We develop ReuScope, a protocol for auditing data reuse and evaluation sensitivity, using Capsule Vision 2024 as a case study. It combines measurements of data relationships with two comparisons: changing the evaluation population while holding predictions fixed, and changing training data while holding evaluation fixed. Byte-identical files cross the public training-validation boundary, and all 41 Kvasir-Capsule recordings that contribute frames occur in both partitions. Shared source recordings establish cross-split overlap; missing cross-recording patient identifiers prevent counting unique shared patients. Across ten paired seeds, removing all training rows attributed to Kvasir-Capsule, plus five rows from other sources flagged as near-matches to it, lowers public-validation balanced accuracy from 82.5% to 61.2%. Evaluating the same fitted models on the validation rows of the other sources reverses the comparison: removal improves balanced accuracy by 1.38 percentage points. The public-validation drop measures sensitivity to source removal, not an amount of leakage-induced inflation. Matched controls show that sample size and class counts alone do not explain the observed score differences. An exploratory experiment removes the training neighbors of validation frames that have close training matches, or equally many distant training rows, and yields a difference-in-differences estimate, relative to matched unflagged fram

1e494d494eefe48ca476d464.title_original: X-World 1.6: Building Controllable Virtual Cities with World Models
1e494d494eefe48ca476d464.excerpt: arXiv:2611.00596v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Deploying generative world models for end-to-end closed-loop evaluation and policy learning requires precise scenario control, consistent observations, and sustained generation quality during extended interactions. This report presents X-World 1.6, advancing X-World 1.0 toward a more reliable and versatile driving simulator. The upgraded base model offers finer-grained control over traffic semantics, including traffic lights and road markings, together with improved spatial consistency across cameras. Virtual City capabilities broaden scenario construction through a family of models conditioned on diverse 2D and 3D references, including support for generating multi-camera future videos from a single image. An enhanced post-training framework enables efficient causal, few-step generation with stronger temporal coherence, better quality retention over longer rollouts, and improved alignment with human preferences. We also introduce a dedicated evaluation suite to support systematic assessment and guide model iteration. Together, these upgrades expand the scenarios X-World can simulate and improve the efficiency and reliability of its generated observations, supporting broader use in autonomous-driving development.

6df7bbddec305c9c7face471.title_original: AI Data Analysis: A New Approach - Multi-engine Joint State Data Analysis
6df7bbddec305c9c7face471.excerpt: arXiv:2611.00807v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: AI data analysis today is three fragmented worlds: LLMs understand semantics but cannot compute; BI aggregates precisely but is stateless; ML processes large-scale data on a stateful kernel but lacks semantics. This paper proposes a combination mechanism, named Multi-engine Joint State Data Analysis, that fills a still-open gap - the multi-engine joint context: the data context is embedded into LLM conversational analysis, where the LLM serves only as the semantic, reasoning, and orchestration layer (not computation) and connects four engines through the 1M context window - Python and R ML kernels, SQL over relational databases, Cypher over graph databases - yielding two multiplications, "semantics and precise computation" and "relational and graph", under enterprise-grade governance. The novelty is a four-dimensional coordinate system: horizontal (engine kinds), vertical (state flow - the watershed), spatial (business generalization), temporal (iterative convergence); a deterministic grounding method (one-shot injection of schema.json + notes.md, M+S) carries the spatial and temporal dimensions. Empirically, all four dimensions are substantiated: horizontally, four engines are quantified - SQL, Cypher (96.5% on CypherBench movie), ML in Python and R (TabReD weather); vertically, state flows across engines and grounding is reused across kernels; spatially, SQL generalizes across three business databases - AdventureWorks 91.3

61f78805664bdbceec1d3d25.title_original: Towards Robust Long-Lived Agents: Benchmarking Experience Lifecycles in Evolving Environments
61f78805664bdbceec1d3d25.excerpt: arXiv:2611.05450v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: As agents become more capable, they are moving beyond one-off tasks toward sustained assistance across successive user goals. Such assistance requires agents to discover how unfamiliar environments work, reuse what they learn across tasks, and keep that experience current as environments evolve. Existing benchmarks increasingly study experience reuse and adaptation, but provide limited insight into which parts of accumulated experience agents revise, retain, or lose. To address this gap, we introduce ReScopeBench, a benchmark for the experience lifecycle across 18 interactive environments. It distinguishes structural experience about how an environment is organized and accessed from rule experience about reusable principles and constraints that guide decisions across tasks. To study how experience is acquired, reused, and revised, we propose an experience-first construction approach. It builds task streams around shared experience and introduces silent environmental changes. We evaluate task performance and track changes in saved experience throughout each stream. Across 20 models, we find that retained experience improves task performance, but agents struggle to keep it current as environments change. Even when the required experience is correctly recorded, agents do not always complete tasks successfully. These findings identify selective maintenance and effective use as complementary challenges for long-lived agents.

fa82d664a82e9f90ca0ebbb4.title_original: Reglos: A Self-Evolving Personal Memory Agent with Recursive Self-Improvement
fa82d664a82e9f90ca0ebbb4.excerpt: arXiv:2611.06049v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Personal agents draw on past conversations to tailor their responses to each user. Their memory systems store and update what each user says, and coding agents now also rewrite the harness that turns this memory into the model's context. Such patches risk overfitting, because one tested only on the failures it targets can fix those cases and help nowhere else. We present Reglos, a personal memory agent that tests whether harness changes help beyond the failures they were written to fix. Its self-evolving memory adds to each user's append-only record with every conversation, as new preferences supersede old ones and facts can be forgotten. Its harness improves through recursive self-improvement, in which a coding agent proposes patches from failure traces and a critic from a second model family screens each one for benchmark gaming. After the harness is frozen, each further patch is tested on users the loop has not seen. With the same backbone behind every system, Reglos outperforms state-of-the-art memory systems such as Mem0, MemOS and EverOS, reaching 67.7% and 84.0% on PersonaMem-v2 and LongMemEval-S with Qwen3.8-27B, and 62.1% and 87.2% with GPT-5.6 Luna.

cb4a223c11abb890f44c6f70.title_original: Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning via Epigraph-Form Guided Exploration
cb4a223c11abb890f44c6f70.excerpt: arXiv:2611.07066v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Discovering cooperative behavior in multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) is challenging due to the combinatorial complexity of joint state-action spaces, which hinders the emergence of coordinated behaviors from trial-and-error alone. Intrinsic rewards are often used to aid discovery, but naively combining them with team objectives can distort the learning signal, compromising task performance. In this paper, we propose EFXPLORER, a constrained exploration framework that maximizes exploration objectives subject to a constraint that preserves established task performance. We solve the resulting problem using an epigraph reformulation that introduces adaptive exploration budgets. This approach separates intrinsic rewards from task objectives and regulates exploration through task feasibility. To further encourage diverse and temporally extended exploration, we incorporate a successor distance-based intrinsic reward that captures long-horizon dependencies. Empirically, our method outperforms strong baselines and induces novel cooperative strategies across SMAX, VMAS, and MPE benchmark suites.

71bd8b5dbbdb0adb2b8a1dcf.title_original: Whom to Trust About the Unseen: How Language Models Weigh Spiritual and Scientific Testimony
71bd8b5dbbdb0adb2b8a1dcf.excerpt: arXiv:2611.08855v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Much of what people believe about the unseen, from germs to spirits, rests on testimony that cannot be checked. We ask how six language models weigh such testimony when it concerns the spiritual and when it concerns the natural, using two paradigms with human data and one new design. In all three, models treat the spiritual as a separate epistemic domain. It has its own credible sources. People credit an obscure New-Age statement more when a scientist says it, while models credit it more from a spiritual leader and switch to the scientist once the statement uses the vocabulary of physics. It has its own standard for an adequate answer. When a trusted expert calls the mechanism behind a belief a mystery, people lose confidence in religious and scientific beliefs, while models prompted as those same people lose it for science and keep it for religion. And credibility earned elsewhere does not readily carry into it. When a fictional forecaster builds a record on checkable river predictions, five models extend that record to hidden natural causes and almost none of it to spiritual ones, and every model trusts the forecaster less about natural causes once the forecaster credits a river spirit. For four of the five models this gap is not a floor effect. It remains when they answer as residents of a village where spirits are taken to exist and rate the spiritual claims well above the bottom of the scale. For the fifth the gap close

4f31150082eb22387261f264.title_original: PhysioWave-T: Token-Efficient Wavelet Foundation Models for Biosignals
4f31150082eb22387261f264.excerpt: arXiv:2611.08969v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present PhysioWave-T, a token-efficient wavelet foundation model family for EEG, ECG, and sEMG. Dynamic scale folding recombines $J+1$ wavelet subbands before tokenization, reducing the sequence from $(J+1)CS$ to $CS$ tokens for $J$ decomposition levels, $C$ channels, and $S$ temporal patches. Route-specific front ends and learned channel-name embeddings allow one Transformer per modality to handle diverse montages and sampling rates. Unseen configurations reuse the pre-trained backbone through a lightweight front end.
