1e4dd55b41f1522783f30046.title_original: CrossProjection: Benchmarking Spatial Grounding across Projection and Section Views
1e4dd55b41f1522783f30046.excerpt: arXiv:2608.00473v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Plans, elevations, and sections describe a three-dimensional structure through incomplete projections that change how an entity is drawn, not only where it is seen from. Reading them means deciding which entities correspond across views and recovering where they lie. We introduce CrossProjection, a benchmark that uses architectural drawings to test whether vision-language models (VLMs) can turn correspondence decisions into geometric answers. Its tasks cover cross-view matching, projection registration, and novel-section prediction, with outputs ranging from judgments and candidate selection to free region boxes and directed section cuts. For inverse section localization, we introduce, to our knowledge, the first VLM benchmark protocol that accepts any cut within an expert-adjudicated band of compatible positions and checks the viewing direction separately. Manually annotated drawings and BIM-derived views provide 33,788 questions from 46 buildings, and we evaluate 22 VLMs on a common set of 2,763. Strong selection or reproduction does not imply cross-view localization: on 100 matched region targets, the best model redraws 98 marked boxes but localizes only 59 across views. Section cuts remain far from expert level, with the leading model trailing two architects by 51.9 and 67.4 percentage points on shared Natural and BIM line questions. 7feb5c6f17fdb014f1141352.title_original: Beyond Statistical Priors: Architecture-Agnostic Data-Free Knowledge Distillation via Unified Explicit Semantics
7feb5c6f17fdb014f1141352.excerpt: arXiv:2608.09287v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Data-Free Knowledge Distillation (DFKD) transfers knowledge from a pretrained teacher model to a compact student model by synthesizing semantically informative data, eliminating the need for access to the original training dataset. Existing DFKD methods rely heavily on architecture-specific statistical priors (e.g., Batch Normalization statistics) to guide data synthesis; however, such architecture-dependent priors are often absent in modern architectures such as Vision Transformers (ViTs), resulting in degraded semantic quality of the synthesized data and consequently catastrophic performance degradation. In this paper, we propose UniDFKD, a unified data-free knowledge distillation framework that replaces architecture-specific statistics with explicit, architecture-agnostic semantic priors. UniDFKD governs the entire synthesis-distillation pipeline along three dimensions: (1) Categorical Semantic Conditioning (CSC) defines what to synthesize by persistently modulating the generator with language-derived embeddings to capture semantic diversity; (2) Spatial Semantic Anchoring (SSA) regularizes where evidence belongs by anchoring the teacher's spatial attributions to a Gaussian prior; and (3) Spatial Semantic Distillation (SSD) controls how knowledge is transferred by explicitly aligning teacher-student spatial evidence alongside predictions. Extensive experiments across CNNs and ViTs demonstrate that UniDFKD sets a new

410820de11d10108e94a0110.title_original: Semantic Prism: Generative Segmentation with an Explicit Semantic-Image Interface
410820de11d10108e94a0110.excerpt: arXiv:2608.11537v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Conditional image generators can render segmentation maps as semantic RGB images, but color drift and boundary mixing can undermine direct decoding. Hierarchical Generator Evidence Alignment (HGEA) combines spatially aligned multilevel features from the VAE encoder of the generator with the input image, generated semantic image, and interface probabilities to predict additive corrections to these logits. Contextual Interface Hierarchy Disagreement (C-IHD) combines pointwise uncertainty, local context, and interface-refinement disagreement in a fixed score for ranking pixel errors, without an auxiliary predictor or an additional network pass. On the 500-image Cityscapes validation set, Semantic Prism achieves 72.07% mean mIoU, improving on direct-interface decoding by 11.39 percentage points. Extensive capacity-matched ablations show higher mean mIoU for multilevel refinement than for flat and single-level alternatives. The Cityscapes-trained model transfers to ACDC Dataset, achieving 46.89% mIoU without target-domain adaptation. Beyond Cityscapes, on

078070736f81102d433401a5.title_original: GEM: A Generative Embedding Model Bridging Reasoning and Retrieval
078070736f81102d433401a5.excerpt: arXiv:2608.13200v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Modern LLMs excel at reasoning and instruction following, enabling users to express increasingly complex information needs. However, existing retrievers largely rely on matching surface-level relevance, creating a growing gap between the evolving nature of user queries and how the queries are interpreted by retrievers. In this paper, we present GEM, a generative embedding model that augments retrieval by leveraging its internal knowledge to reason about user intent and relevance criteria prior to embedding. GEM unifies generation and embedding in a sequential manner, where encoding can be conceptually viewed as processing only one additional token during autoregressive generation. Unlike conventional query expansion, GEM learns to produce embeddings aligned with its reasoning, moving beyond surface-level matching. Furthermore, the generative nature allows GEM to be prompted like standard instruction-tuned LLMs and enables test-time compute scaling for retrieval. Compared with a non-reasoning variant of the same backbone, GEM achieves approximately 35% relative improvement in nDCG@10 on BRIGHT, a benchmark of challenging queries requiring reasoning, and 70% in p-MRR on FollowIR, a benchmark evaluating retrievers' ability to understand and follow user instructions. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of activating an embedding model's internal reasoning capabilities to improve retrieval. Our code and model are publ

5e8514d1f46b484d7c7f2dec.title_original: Does Latent Planning Survive Point Clouds? Action-Conditioned JEPA World Models for Geometric Observations and Goals
5e8514d1f46b484d7c7f2dec.excerpt: arXiv:2608.29434v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Latent action world models let agents plan new behaviors at test time by predicting how actions change the environment, and joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) do so by forecasting future latent states rather than pixels. Yet nearly all such models see the world through a camera, even though robotic manipulation is fundamentally geometric: in robotics goals for manipulation are traditionally specified by target object poses, not by images of the object once placed. We ask whether latent planning survives a shift from appearance to geometry, on the observation side as well as on the goal specifications side. To answer this, we extend the stable-worldmodel evaluation platform with simulated LiDAR-style raycast point clouds as a new sensor modality, and adapt three JEPA designs to point clouds: a frozen-encoder model built on Utonia features, a distribution-prior model based on LeWM, and an action-sensitive model based on Delta-JEPA. We further introduce a goal-encoding mechanism that constructs the goal latent from the current latent and a 3D target pose, removing the need for goal images or goal point clouds. A comparative evaluation of the different anti-collapse mechanisms shows that point-cloud world models can match their image-based counterparts, demonstrating that the modality shift from appearance to geometry is achievable. All models are released as open weights with open-source training and inferen

29b972a08255e5a99f77d676.title_original: AutoXRD: Autonomous Large Language Model Agents and Comprehensive Evaluation for Powder X-Ray Diffraction Analysis
29b972a08255e5a99f77d676.excerpt: arXiv:2609.00070v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Powder X-ray diffraction (XRD) is a foundational technique for structural and phase characterization in materials science, yet automating its analysis and evaluating it end-to-end remains challenging. Doing so requires an agent to interpret diffraction patterns, run refinement software, manage strongly coupled parameters in a physically meaningful order, and assess both numerical fit quality and physical validity. We propose AutoXRD, an LLM agent framework that organizes powder XRD analysis into refinement stages, uses diffraction diagnostics to select actions, and checks the resulting fits against crystallographic and physical criteria. We further introduce XRDBench with two complementary tracks. XRDBench-QA contains 100 tasks assessing scientific reasoning and decision-making, whereas XRDBench-E2E contains 34 end-to-end workflows requiring data interpretation, crystallographic software execution, iterative refinement, evidence preservation, and reporting. Across 1,340 runs of ten recent LLMs, models average only 57.8 out of 100, falling from 61.9 on XRDBench-QA to 53.7 on XRDBench-E2E. At the task level, they perform best on refinement-history assessment and result acceptance, but remain substantially weaker on refinement-action selection, phase quantification, indexing, and Rietveld refinement. Among individual models, GPT-5.6 Sol achieves the highest overall score of 81.1, GPT-5.6 Terra scores highest on XRDBench-E

fd075a38ac70a9ff7d4671ad.title_original: Untangling the Mechanisms of Misleading Context in Medical Question Answering
fd075a38ac70a9ff7d4671ad.excerpt: arXiv:2609.02754v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large language models now answer medical questions with expert-level performance. However, the context these systems act on can be misleading, and misleading context can corrupt a model's medical judgment. To understand how misleading context corrupts this judgment, we examine the model's susceptibility to the context, disclosure of it, mechanism of corrupted reasoning, and monitorability of the decision. On the medical reasoning subset of MedMisBench, a clinician-reviewed question-answering benchmark of 8,627 questions, we inject two types of misleading context cues, fabricated evidence and a bare assertion. We test three reasoning models, two that expose their full reasoning trace and one frontier model that exposes only its response. All three are more susceptible to the assertion than to the fabricated evidence, adopting the asserted answer 10 to 27 points more often. The misleading cues are disclosed in 81 to 98% of traces but only 7 to 90% of responses, and the assertion is disclosed less often than evidence based cues. Resampling from reasoning traces without disclosure shows the two cues corrupt reasoning differently, evidence entering early and accumulating while the assertion redirects the conclusion near its end. An LLM monitor catches 78% of corrupted decisions at 5% false positives when reading an open model's trace with guidance, against at most 32% from any response. The misleading context that models ar

3433eb9ba4672c594b5f7379.title_original: From Synthetic Priors to Model Behavior: Structural Coverage in Tabular Foundation Models
3433eb9ba4672c594b5f7379.excerpt: arXiv:2609.06912v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Tabular foundation models (TFMs) are commonly pretrained on large collections of procedurally generated synthetic tasks, yet it remains unclear how well these synthetic pretraining priors support the downstream tasks on which the models are evaluated. We study this from a distribution-level attribution perspective. We recover or reconstruct the synthetic data generators of four TFMs and compare their generated tasks with datasets from two widely used tabular benchmarks. Each dataset is represented by a common set of structural descriptors capturing schema, feature distributions, dependence structure, response properties, and feature--response relationships. We then measure how broadly and repeatedly each synthetic prior reaches benchmark tasks using structural coverage and normalized density, and examine whether stronger local support is associated with better predictive performance. We find substantial differences across synthetic pretraining priors: some generators provide broader and denser support for benchmark tasks than others. Moreover, stronger synthetic-to-benchmark support is generally associated with better relative model performance, although this association is largely driven by the model with the broadest support and mostly disappears once each model's average support is removed. These results suggest that structural coverage provides a useful diagnostic for characterizing synthetic pretraining priors, wh

ec11ea59e9fbe1edb1ab1b01.title_original: Constrained Online Learning with Noisy Constraint Values
ec11ea59e9fbe1edb1ab1b01.excerpt: arXiv:2609.06921v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study online convex optimization with time-varying constraints when the constraint values are observed only through noise. In each round the learner picks an action, pays a convex loss, and incurs a convex constraint value that should be nonpositive; it then receives unbiased estimates of the loss and constraint gradients, and an unbiased observation of the constraint value whose error has bounded variance. Performance is measured against the best fixed action in hindsight among those that satisfy every constraint, and violation by the largest total overspend over any interval of consecutive rounds, which we call budget violation. Our algorithm, LEDGER, has $O(\sqrt T)$ expected regret and $O(\sqrt{T\log T})$ expected budget violation over $T$ rounds, uses one projection per round, and needs no strictly feasible action. The logarithm cannot be removed: with Gaussian noise of fixed positive variance, every algorithm with $O(\sqrt T)$ worst-case regret has worst-case budget violation of order at least $\sqrt{T\log T}$, even if only the final total overspend is counted, and budget violation $O(\sqrt T)$ forces linear regret. When violation is instead the sum of the positive parts of the per-round constraint values (hard violation), no algorithm keeps both expected regret and expected hard violation sublinear if the noise distribution is not fixed, even for affine constraints. With a fixed and known Gaussian noise law o

bcbca44fd1d8d8c2f08b9ee4.title_original: SWE-Proof: Can Language Models Resolve Real-World Issues with Machine-Checked Proofs?
bcbca44fd1d8d8c2f08b9ee4.excerpt: arXiv:2609.21190v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Ensuring the correctness of LLM-generated code is a core challenge for modern software engineering. Benchmarks for agentic code generation check correctness with held-out test suites, which are inherently incomplete and increasingly susceptible to memorization. Formal verification avoids both problems, but existing work covers only standalone tasks whose specifications are given as input, not real issues, which touch large repositories and state intent in vague natural language. We present BenchProofer, a pipeline that turns a coding task with a known correct patch into a formally verified one: it writes a specification for the new code, summarizes the existing functions that code calls with axioms, and admits an instance only after mechanical and adversarial gates agree. Applying it to SWE-bench Verified yields SWE-Proof, 500 real issues whose correctness is formally verified rather than tested, and it extends to SWE-bench Pro. Evaluating Claude Opus 4.8, we find that verification catches what tests miss: nearly a third of test-passing patches admit counterexamples, which a structured natural-language specification does not fix, while a correct formal one lifts resolution from 85% to 95%. Writing that specification is the hard part: an agent that must write its own gains nothing over an unaided baseline, and only 56% of those specifications pass our audit. The usual failure is faithfulness, where a specification const

3abf6572c279469a2cdd2ca9.title_original: RLVR$^{2}$: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rubric-based Ranking
3abf6572c279469a2cdd2ca9.excerpt: arXiv:2609.23457v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) is expanding from tasks with well-defined correctness signals, such as mathematics and code, toward multifaceted quality requirements specified by multi-dimensional rubrics. Since policy optimization consumes one scalar per rollout, rubric-based pipelines must map multiple criterion scores into a scalar reward. This aggregation is often treated as score scaling, but it implicitly determines how quality dimensions trade off during training. The prevailing practice, normalizing each criterion and taking a linear combination, assumes that cardinal score differences are comparable across criteria and that gains on one criterion compensate for failures on another; both assumptions are unreliable when criteria are semantically heterogeneous. We propose Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rubric-based Ranking (RLVR$^2$), a verifiable ranking paradigm for rubric-based RLVR. For each criterion, RLVR$^2$ converts rubric scores into criterion-specific within-group ordinal outcomes, recovers a latent utility from the resulting comparison matrix, and merges these utilities into one training signal. By retaining only within-group ordering and discarding raw score magnitudes, RLVR$^2$ avoids calibrating heterogeneous rubric scales. It further supports objective-preserving attribute adjustment: auxiliary attributes that correlate with observed rankings but are not training objec

1a7b49daa226a2a6edb3be42.title_original: Resolving State-Representation Mismatch: State-Space Visual Reasoning for Open-Loop VLA Planning
1a7b49daa226a2a6edb3be42.excerpt: arXiv:2609.33412v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Despite rapid progress in vision-language-action (VLA) models, existing reasoning paradigms still face a fundamental \emph{state-representation mismatch} in open-loop planning. Given only an initial observation, models must internally simulate action-conditioned state transitions, whereas text-, pixel-, and latent-space reasoning can suffer from lossy spatial compression, error-accumulating visual generation, and bypass of intermediate latent tokens, respectively, undermining reliable long-horizon planning. We propose \textbf{State-Space Visual Reasoning} (SSVR), which decouples static visual context, language constraints, and a recurrent latent state. SSVR encodes the initial image and instruction once, then conditions each action prediction on the latent state and updates it with an action-conditioned GRU. Using Qwen2.5-VL as the backbone, SSVR achieves 99.5/99.6, 96.3/98.0, and 83.9/90.6 EM/PR on FrozenLake, Maze, and MiniBehavior, substantially outperforming prior methods. Extensive experiments support the effectiveness of recurrent state modeling for VLA open-loop planning across input transformations and transfer settings. By reusing static visual-textual context and updating a compact recurrent state, SSVR supports efficient multi-step inference, achieving up to $98.58\times$ faster Maze decoding rollouts than the evaluated baselines with the prefix cache prebuilt.

0f9b279e83ad87bcda029a3d.title_original: ContextAdapt: Evaluating Contextual Adaptation and Value Alignment in LLMs
0f9b279e83ad87bcda029a3d.excerpt: arXiv:2609.38260v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Values such as honesty, autonomy, and confidentiality are often regarded as general principles underpinning AI alignment. However, what it means to act in accordance with these values can depend on the context in which a decision is made. In this paper, we ask whether large language models (LLMs) appropriately adapt the application of a value across professional settings, while remaining consistent when contextual changes do not alter the relevant professional norm. To study this, we introduce ContextAdapt, an evaluation framework covering honesty, autonomy, and confidentiality across medicine, law, finance, and national security. Drawing on primary-source professional and regulatory documents, we construct a value x domain framework and use this to develop scenarios testing both default professional rules and recognised exceptions. We evaluate 12 LLMs on both the actions they recommend and the justifications they provide. In our main experiment, models achieve 95.9% mean action-level appropriateness, although the use of the correct domain-specific justification varies substantially across models, from 25.6% to 76.9%. In a separate factorial experiment, explicitly naming the professional domain and changing the role of the model have limited effect on behaviour, whereas changing stakes produces a 10.3-point average difference between low- and high-stakes conditions and severe but localised failures. These results show

1ddf9e608f5457536537715a.title_original: Exploring the Hidden Cost of the World Around AI Agents
1ddf9e608f5457536537715a.excerpt: arXiv:2609.38469v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Agent benchmarks test what agents can do in environments that are built for their tasks. Deployed agents work in the real world where other people and tools can change the state. An agent booking a flight may receive a message from someone else to change the destination, or a booking tool may fail without saying whether the ticket was purchased. We present BACKDROP, which asks how much of an agent's capability in a clean world survives in a non-cooperative world. BACKDROP takes a task along with the agent's execution environment, and plants four everyday hazards in its environment, one at a time and all together. Each hazard tests a different behavior. Authority: does a non-author actor instruction, from anyone who did not author the task, override the user's goal? Injection: does text planted in a record redirect the agent? Boundary: does the agent make changes in an app the user's task did not require? Fault: after a write fails without saying whether it landed, does the agent check before it retries? Across 3,678 variants and 16 models, the average pass rate falls from 69.5% to 31.3% once all four hazards are present; the strongest models fall furthest (Claude Fable 5.1 from 96.6% to 56.0%). The gap is consistent throughout all 16 models. BACKDROP formalizes these gaps and shows how an agent's score in a task's world is a ceiling on real-world performance.

13f99df98c88a297483c4194.title_original: Motion Without State: Probing Dynamical Consistency and Conditioning Bias in Video Models
13f99df98c88a297483c4194.excerpt: arXiv:2610.05135v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Image-to-video models serve as visual world priors whose plausible motion departs from physical simulation. We ask what dynamical structure replaces forward state propagation in generated motion, and how it biases quantitative physics evaluation. Holding law and initial state fixed, we vary visible geometry, prompt wording, and clip length across nine models and compare tracked trajectories against simulator rollouts. Generated motion splits into local visual cues and global boundary control, omitting the propagating physical state between them. Locally, tempo-normalized speed follows track undulations with a 15{\deg}-41{\deg} phase lead toward steepest descent as mean slope barely accelerates the ball, showing short memory of past slope. Local responses fail to compose: no single contact law describes a model's bounces (prescribed, self-calibrated on single-deflector contacts, or fitted in-sample), and balls clear 43 of 49 barriers above release height under an outcome-free prompt. Globally, naming the catch tray lifts arrival 14-76 percentage points above post-contact simulator rollouts, and event duration scales near-linearly with clip length, making apparent gravity 5.6-7.3 times higher in 3 s than in 8 s clips. These patterns persist on photographed first frames, motivating neutral-prompt controls, exit-state rollouts, and tempo-normalized metrics.

60a8c8e27275e77af56b5a59.excerpt: arXiv:2610.09108v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Policy learning drives many of the most consequential and heavily-invested applications of reinforcement learning today. Yet the core optimization problem it rests on (maximizing expected return) is notoriously non-convex, even under a direct policy parameterization, and the field has largely responded by avoiding it: optimizing convex surrogate approximations of the return under trust-region constraints (NPG, TRPO, PPO, AWR). We show that this seemingly unstructured problem is not actually structureless. In log-density-ratio coordinates $y := \log[\pi/\pi_n]$, the exact per-iteration objective, computable via per-decision importance sampling (PDIS), is a difference-of-convex-constrained difference-of-convex (DC-constrained DC) program. This structure lets us move beyond surrogate approximations: it recovers CPI, NPG, TRPO, and AWR as special cases along interpretable axes, and it opens a multi-step axis $k$ that couples consecutive decisions. We solve the per-iteration program with sequential convex programming (SCP), the standard solver for difference-of-convex problems, and establish inner-loop descent and limit-point stationarity for the theoretical algorithm, together with a conditional outer-loop performance bound. Empirically, multi-step Convex-Concave RL (CCRL) wins on diagnostic MDPs where credit must propagate across a horizon (its advantage growing with the dependency length), is competitive with a tuned PPO

1d9db354f035d61639c6bf43.title_original: SPLICE: Sparse Physics Library Identification and Compositional Expansion
1d9db354f035d61639c6bf43.excerpt: arXiv:2610.17029v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Neural operator splitting composes a library of neural operators, one per physical mechanism, into zero-shot simulators of new equations. Existing approaches, however, require these mechanisms and their labels to be specified in advance. We ask whether a pretrained library can instead be adapted and grown from unlabeled trajectories in which multiple mechanisms act simultaneously. We introduce SPLICE, a framework that discovers operators without mechanism labels on mixture data. The contributions of the candidate operators to each trajectory are inferred by solving a convex optimization problem. A calibrated test then assigns each discovered operator the mechanism it implements. Failure cases are also detectable, when the library lacks the required physics or when mechanisms are insufficiently separable, and growth recovers only mechanisms the pretrained network represents. Across one and two dimensional systems, the discovered operators recover mechanisms from unlabeled mixtures and compose into zero-shot simulators of unseen equations; on Navier-Stokes they compose close to their supervised counterparts.

739e920bcad4c561638b4f1e.title_original: Urbex: Agentic Spatial Grounding for City-Scale 3D Scenes
739e920bcad4c561638b4f1e.excerpt: arXiv:2610.18356v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: City-scale 3D grounding is commonly formulated as candidate ranking, which requires precomputed instance proposals and becomes inefficient in large outdoor scenes. We propose Urbex, an agentic vision-language framework that instead casts grounding as active spatial search. Urbex represents a city-scale 3D scene as an interactive multi-view environment, allowing a VLM agent to query landmarks, zoom into local regions, render oblique views, and commit a grounded bounding box. We optimize this tool-use policy with reinforcement learning on CityRefer, using smooth localization rewards and lightweight shaping rewards for efficient exploration. Experiments show that Urbex achieves the best Hit@1 and IoU on CityRefer, supports candidate-free grounding without ground-truth boxes, and is substantially faster than the strongest city-scale ranking baseline. Zero-shot results on STPLS3D-Refer further indicate improved cross-scene robustness.

8eb06be4c3d267834ee1a22f.title_original: Find the Fungible: Variable-Resolution Tokenization that Compacts Semantics with a Granularity Dial as a VLM "Catalyst"
8eb06be4c3d267834ee1a22f.excerpt: arXiv:2610.18690v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Efficient vision-language models should preserve a useful representation of the whole image, even under tight budgets. However, aggressive pruning or indiscriminate merging can erase critical details and disrupt the spatial structure. We thus propose Varest, which maximizes semantic fungibility: tokens describing coherent content can be summarized together with minimal information loss. Object boundaries distilled from a visual foundation model guide grouping, while text localization protects details needed for reading. At lower budgets, Varest merges the image into coarser semantic regions, while maintaining full spatial coverage. After early language decoder layers process this representation, a learned selector prunes visual tokens that later layers no longer need, reducing repeated access to already integrated information. Across three LLaVA backbones and 13 benchmarks, Varest outperforms 10 training-free and 5 trained baselines in mean performance retention at every evaluated budget, preserving 86.10-92.33% of uncompressed performance using only 5.56% of tokens. This SOTA performance further generalizes to modern VLMs like Qwen3.8-27B.

c783bac0a4dc5bc1bb9e9c69.title_original: Red-Teaming Multi-Agent Attacks for Loss-of-Control Risks
c783bac0a4dc5bc1bb9e9c69.excerpt: arXiv:2610.24052v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: AI agents are growing more capable and persistent, and are being deployed in ever larger numbers. As more start collaborating, AI control measures must remain effective when they covertly collude on a harmful objective. We introduce MiniLab, a synthetic series of live services and codebases (5 interconnected services, 249 benign tasks, 8 attack objectives), adapted from internal AI deployment infrastructure. We demonstrate distributed attacks, in which different agents carry out separate attack fragments, and how their covertness evades frontier monitors when reading their trajectories individually. We show how distributed attacks spread across diverse contexts and harmful objectives through 16 human-optimized attacks (weight exfiltration, unmonitored rogue deployment, permission elevation, and more). A frontier monitor, GPT-5.6 Sol, reading each agent separately flags only 3.4% of successful distributed attacks, compared with 82.4% when a single agent carries out the same side task. Individual attacks can also be composed into longer attack sequences toward a greater loss-of-control outcome, without any individual agent being flagged. 66b5bab3b348879fcba8fc40.title_original: One Evaluation Is Enough: Inversion-Free Image Editing with Trajectory Correction
66b5bab3b348879fcba8fc40.excerpt: arXiv:2610.30827v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Real-image editing commonly relies on inversion and iterative sampling, while efficient one-step editors often stabilize a large update by estimating and averaging editing fields at multiple noise levels. We ask a stricter question: is a single temporal field evaluation sufficient for reliable inversion-free editing? Our answer rests on a previously underused duality in a variance-preserving (VP) one-step model: one source-target query at a shared noisy state simultaneously determines a local angular semantic tangent and a clean endpoint displacement. We integrate the tangent over the analytically known remaining VP angle to obtain a nominal one-step transport, and use the endpoint displacement to correct its long-horizon extrapolation through a constrained projection. This transport-first, correction-second construction yields Endpoint-Calibrated Transport (ECT), a closed-form, training-free editor requiring only one noise level, two text conditions packed into one denoiser batch, and one latent update. ECT requires no image inversion, trajectory integration, second temporal observation, or iterative optimization, and can be directly applied to pretrained epsilon-prediction VP one-step generators. Across the reported benchmark settings, ECT delivers stable gains in editing quality within an extremely short editing time.

c61b0a88e74b1abdb3f5b145.title_original: A Mathematical Theory of the Jacobian Lens
c61b0a88e74b1abdb3f5b145.excerpt: arXiv:2610.31955v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Recent work from Anthropic introduced a new interpretability tool, called the Jacobian lens (J-lens, Gurnee et al. 2026). This method identified linear directions in the hidden states of frontier language models that had properties reminiscent of working-memory-like representations. However, it is unclear what mechanistic properties of such features make them detectable by the J-lens. To this end, we introduce a mathematical theory of the J-lens and show that it preferentially identifies coherent features--directions that act like leading, spatially coherent finite-time Lyapunov modes. Small perturbations along these directions maximally amplify across layers, remain roughly constant across token positions, and are consistent across different contexts. While we are agnostic to whether these properties are necessarily associated with a "Global Workspace'', the analytically derived preferences of the J-lens nevertheless explain prior empirical results. We validate our analysis on a Bayes filter and a toy transformer, each optimally predicting next tokens emitted from a Hidden Markov Model (HMM). We show how modulating task parameters that change the coherence of features in the Bayes filter correspondingly and predictively modulates the response of the J-lens applied to both model classes. a84f5d464552a97d2f3e8e0b.title_original: EvolveMAS: A Unified Self-Evolution Framework for Decentralized Multi-Agent Systems
a84f5d464552a97d2f3e8e0b.excerpt: arXiv:2610.34450v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Decentralized multi-agent systems (MAS) enable large language model agents to interact without centralized control. Agents need to adapt to other agents at test time and reuse accumulated experience to refine their interaction strategies for future interactions across cooperative, mixed-motive, and adversarial settings. However, existing approaches often develop adaptation mechanisms for particular interaction settings. This raises a central question: how can decentralized MAS support test-time adaptation and reliable experience reuse across interaction settings? We propose EvolveMAS, a unified self-evolution framework that supports experience-driven adaptation within and across episodes. EvolveMAS pairs each main agent with a dedicated MemoryAgent for test-time memory governance, which maintains isolated Structured Memory outside the main agent's reasoning context. EvolveMAS organizes adaptation into two complementary processes: Within-Episode Online Adaptation and Cross-Episode Knowledge Evolution. During Within-Episode Online Adaptation, MemoryAgent updates episodic, semantic, and working memory from interaction evidence to inform subsequent actions. During Cross-Episode Knowledge Evolution, the main agent uses memory and episode outcomes to distill reusable interaction knowledge comprising partner profiles and interaction strategies for subsequent episodes. 0a354bf726d8316c066227c6.title_original: Ranking Function Generation with LLMs for Termination
0a354bf726d8316c066227c6.excerpt: arXiv:2610.35523v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Ranking functions are a fundamental technique for proving loop termination, but synthesizing them remains challenging and often requires substantial expertise. Despite considerable progress in their automated synthesis, existing approaches remain limited in their effectiveness. We propose RAINFALL, a neuro-symbolic framework that tightly integrates large language models (LLMs) with symbolic verification. To our best knowledge, RAINFALL is the first to employ a generate-verify-refine paradigm for LLM-based ranking function synthesis. RAINFALL formulates ranking function synthesis as a constrained code-completion task, inserting placeholders into the input program that the LLM must fill in four predefined slots per loop. The resulting program is checked by a symbolic verifier. Successful verification yields a valid ranking function, while verification failures produce diagnostics that are translated into natural-language feedback to guide iterative refinement. We evaluate RAINFALL on two public benchmark suites comprising 358 terminating C programs. Using DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, RAINFALL synthesizes verified ranking functions for 333 programs (93.02%), outperforming all evaluated baselines. Notably, it solves 22 more programs than PROTON 2.1, the winner of the SV-COMP 2026 Termination Category. c12635fc4a17c6e10da9cdf9.title_original: ResCom: Activation Residual Compensation for Large Language Model Quantization
c12635fc4a17c6e10da9cdf9.excerpt: arXiv:2610.35955v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Low-bit weight--activation quantization reduces the memory and computation needed to deploy large language models, but activation rounding can still degrade accuracy after calibration. Reconstruction from rounded inputs cannot distinguish activations within the same quantization bin. We propose ResCom, a low-rank correction that uses the activation rounding residual to compensate for the resulting layer-output error. An output-aware calibration procedure selects residual directions by their contribution to output reconstruction and computes the correction in closed form, without gradient training or updates to the calibrated weights. On Llama-3-8B with 4-bit weights and activations, rank-32 attention corrections reduce WikiText-2 perplexity from 7.708 to 7.147, improve MMLU by 2.89 percentage points, and raise five-shot GSM8K accuracy from 23.96 to 36.16 percent. Evaluations on models from 1B to 70B parameters and on held-out C4 test the method beyond this setting. The evaluated FP32 implementation adds 2.25 percent to 4K prefill time; a separate compact-storage implementation retains a 27.7 percent peak-memory reduction relative to FP16.

6fc4d919d20925ada5819022.title_original: Atom as an Agent: Emergent Order by Collective Predictive Coding
6fc4d919d20925ada5819022.excerpt: arXiv:2610.36673v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: What is the intrinsic reason of emergence of macroscopic order parameter out of microscopic systems? In this article, we apply to physics the collective predictive coding (CPC), the theory of language/symbol emergence. As our language emerges out of our human communications, physical macroscopic order parameter emerges out of communications among atoms --- each atom is regarded as an agent who predicts each other's behavior through inference. We present three examples of classical spin systems: two-dimensional ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic Ising models, a two-dimensional spin model with competing stripe orders, and the fully connected Sherrington--Kirkpatrick spin-glass model. In all of these examples, proper macroscopic order parameters including the replica overlap emerge automatically through communication informatics of CPC, only from observed spin configurations. We call the learned macroscopic coordinate the collective predictive order. Furthermore, for the ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic Ising models, the equilibrium distribution of the collective predictive order yields an emergent potential with the symmetry and thermal evolution characteristic of a Landau potential. Notably, the emergence of the collective predictive order does not refer to any structure of microscopic Hamiltonians/Lagrangians. Thus our ``Atom-as-an-Agent" (AaaA) principle offers a completely data-driven method for the emergence of

38873498499007173c5f95e3.title_original: Intervenable Concept Dynamics for Video Activity Forecasting
38873498499007173c5f95e3.excerpt: arXiv:2611.00020v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Concept bottleneck models route predictions through human-understandable concepts, making their intermediate states inspectable and editable. Extending this model family to forecasting requires modeling how concept activations evolve over time as objects, actions, and their interactions change, yet existing CBMs ground concepts only in observed inputs and do not forecast their future evolution. We study this problem using videos of ongoing activities and forecast future activities through a named-concept state. We propose TRACE-CBM (Temporal Relational Activity Concept Evolution), which first refines observed concept activations with sparse spatio-temporal graphs. It then recursively predicts future concept states, conditioning each transition on the prior activity distribution, and decodes both observed and predicted states with a shared activity classifier. At inference time, the model supports editing concept values, activity activations, and learned edges without parameter updates, exposing the relational spatio-temporal dependencies used for forecasting. Across multiple datasets, TRACE improves observed-activity accuracy over concept-based methods and stays close to matched black-box forecasters in forecast accuracy. Intervention experiments show that concept edits correct part of the initially incorrect forecasts without flipping initially correct ones, and that activity-belief edits can steer forecasts toward a

16678f18a11becbb3349d3bc.title_original: Demystifying Prompt Stealing Attacks against Synthetic Video
16678f18a11becbb3349d3bc.excerpt: arXiv:2611.00102v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Creators publicly showcase generated content to advertise and sell their work, but these examples may also enable unauthorized reproduction and customization. We study whether an adversary can derive reusable inputs from a single public video for faithful reconstruction and controlled editing, without access to the original prompt or generator. We adapt captioning and prompt optimization approaches to video prompt stealing attacks (PSAs) and find that prompt recovery alone provides limited reconstruction fidelity. Even the original prompt produces different spatial and temporal realizations when the initial noise changes. Using an independent generator enlarges the reconstruction gap, as reusing the original prompt and seed can still produce substantially different videos. We propose V-PSA, which uses a recovered caption and DDIM inversion to construct a reference trajectory under an independent generator. Null-Text Inversion then optimizes per-step unconditional embeddings to reduce deviations from this trajectory during reconstruction. The resulting inputs also guide generation when the caption is modified, supporting edits that change selected content while preserving the target's layout and motion. We construct a benchmark containing 12,000 video-prompt pairs from three victim generators and four prompt sources. V-PSA achieves video-to-video similarity around 0.9 between target and reconstructed videos, substantial

01543eb17040ab16f68f8a85.title_original: Sparse Autoencoder Attribution Graphs Are Decided at the Margin
01543eb17040ab16f68f8a85.excerpt: arXiv:2611.00606v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Interpretability research writes a language model's activation as a weighted sum of learned directions, called features. A sparse autoencoder (SAE) learns the features and gives each a coefficient, its weight in that sum. The SAE's encoder first gives every feature a score. A TopK SAE selects the k features with the largest positive scores and zeroes the rest. A feature's margin is how far its score must move before the selection changes. An intervention on one feature's coefficient changes the encoder scores of the SAE at the next layer. An attribution graph predicts that change from the scores' derivatives with respect to the coefficient, taken before the intervention. The graph keeps the original selection, so it misses every feature that enters or leaves. We propose the margin graph, which adds the predicted change to every score and selects again. When one feature is zeroed in a public pair of Pythia-70M SAEs, the median error of the predicted coefficient change, relative to the true change, falls from 0.739 for the attribution graph to 0.121 for the margin graph. Written back into the model, the margin graph's coefficients predict the change in the model's output on subject verb agreement less accurately than the attribution graph's. Selecting again better predicts which features change, but on the task and pair we tested, not the model's output.

cc0cc850d3cbd3e0d0bb5701.title_original: Lightweight Representation Learning for Low Tucker Rank Tensors
cc0cc850d3cbd3e0d0bb5701.excerpt: arXiv:2611.01168v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Iterative estimators for low Tucker rank tensors, such as HOOI, nuclear-norm proximal and ADMM methods, Frank-Wolfe and scaled gradient descent, form large objects in every iteration: unfoldings, Kronecker operators, full SVDs and ambient iterates. The update uses little of these objects, yet they make memory the limiting resource on large tensors and on edge-sized devices. Remedies for each of these costs are known. However, it is unclear when a rewriting keeps the iterates unchanged, and where it pays off against efficient implementations. We therefore present a trajectory-preserving lightweight evaluation. First, we state exactness as an intertwining relation between the stored state and the reference iteration. Second, we show that three known components satisfy this relation for five estimators: computing only the singular triplets that an update needs, contracting without Kronecker products, and storing sparse-plus-factored states. As a result, the iterates and all guarantees of the reference estimator stay the same. On an A100 GPU, with the input data counted in the memory, lightweight HOOI needs the least memory of 15 HOOI-type methods at every size ($95\times$ less beyond the input than the lightest exact implementation on $800^3$ tensors), and it is the fastest method that reaches the HOOI estimate on the largest tensors. Against efficient public code, ours is faster and lighter for three of five estimators.

06d4951ab066e8d843d8f8f3.excerpt: arXiv:2611.09892v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Recent work on robot manipulation has focused on specialist policies trained on demonstrations. We show that generalist AI models can control manipulators more reliably than specialist policies such as vision-language-action models (VLAs) and world-action models (WAMs). The agent succeeds zero-shot in 104 of 108 real-world trials spanning twelve tasks and three robot instances, reducing failure rates by 20x and 15x relative to strong VLA and WAM baselines. The basic harness supplies no grasping, pushing, or placing skills; the agent develops its own strategies, such as searching for hidden objects, using objects as tools, and calibrating its cameras. With the addition of a persistent memory store, the agent can also learn from experience: an augmented harness with a memory representation that is carried across episodes lowers the failure rate on RoboDojo bimanual manipulation tasks by 4.6x

4939d469269e4d7c20b331d8.title_original: RoadState: A Domain-Prior-Enhanced Vision-Language System for Industrial-Grade Lane-Level Map Updating
4939d469269e4d7c20b331d8.excerpt: arXiv:2611.10746v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Lane-level maps provide foundational structured road information for navigation, intelligent driving, and intelligent transportation systems. We present RoadState, a production-deployed vision-language system that transforms sequential road-scene observations into structured lane-level semantics for Baidu Maps' map-updating pipeline. Its core model, RoadState-VLM, formulates road-scene understanding as autoregressive state estimation, predicting the current structured road state from the previous observation, previous symbolic state, and current observation. To improve semantic consistency and reasoning fidelity across interdependent road-state dimensions, we introduce Geometric Chain-of-Thought (Geo-CoT), which encodes a directed acyclic graph of semantic dependencies as a domain prior. On a real-world dataset, RoadState-VLM achieves 94.33% mean accuracy across six road-state dimensions, outperforming the strongest fine-tuned VLM baseline, with ablations confirming the complementary gains of Geo-CoT and temporal transition context. 3f54b21da8b8f9b0cbe3fa47.title_original: Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization
3f54b21da8b8f9b0cbe3fa47.excerpt: arXiv:2611.12016v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Many real-world applications require language models to internalize knowledge that was absent from pretraining, to incorporate continually updated facts, or to learn new domain skills. We propose Speculative Self-Distillation (SSD), an efficient per-token mixed-policy method for self-distillation. The student generates each rollout by default, while the teacher intervenes only at positions where its next-token distribution substantially diverges from the student's. Unlike off-policy distillation with teacher-generated prefixes, this design keeps training rollouts close to the student's test-time behavior, while avoiding the low-signal states that fully on-policy rollouts drift into. In effect, SSD lets the teacher steer the rollout exactly where the privileged context changes the prediction. On three closed-book QA benchmarks measuring fact recall, knowledge updates, and skill acquisition, SSD nearly matches on-policy distillation while using 38-69% fewer supervised tokens and consistently outperforms off-policy distillation on the held-out test set. b32ffebd46b4cae1cd46eb5e.title_original: From Attack Surface to Defense Architecture: Compositional Security for Agentic Coding Harnesses
b32ffebd46b4cae1cd46eb5e.excerpt: arXiv:2611.13960v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: AI coding harnesses couple language models to shells, filesystems, and network sockets so that agents can resolve issues and run tests. 3926a0a14fe4dc140a073380.title_original: Visual Similarity in Adult Word Extension and Artificial Word Learning
3926a0a14fe4dc140a073380.excerpt: arXiv:2611.14116v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: When two objects share a name, how much does their visual similarity explain, and what do the teaching examples add? Within the taught domain, greater distance was associated with less extension for all eight trained encoders and for the untrained network, so the association cannot be attributed only to what the encoders learned; raw pixels showed no negative association. In post hoc models that let the distance slope vary across images, seven of the eight trained encoders retained a negative estimate and five had 95% intervals entirely below zero; the interval of the reference encoder included zero. Whether trial order changes the distance slope, the frozen primary question, remained inconclusive. Example composition changed extension at comparable distances: after three examples, adults extended a word to 1.1% of superordinate items when the examples were subordinate and to 77.5% when they were superordinate. In artificial learners, words joining more distant categories were learned less accurately for six of the eight trained encoders. 80fc9ee068f3a1a6f20c8375.title_original: Editable Video Context: Mid-Context KV-Cache Reuse for Context-Managing Video LLMs
80fc9ee068f3a1a6f20c8375.excerpt: arXiv:2611.18718v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Context Language Models let a model edit its own context, while Suffix Cache Reuse makes edits to text efficient by adjusting the positions of cached keys for surviving tokens. We extend these ideas to video language models with multimodal rotary position embeddings (M-RoPE). We represent a long video as timestamped segments. After viewing a sparsely sampled version, the model selects segments for decoding at 4x the frame rate, and the remaining segments are removed from its context. Our rebuild method reuses the KV cache of surviving segments by rotating their keys with a single offset shared by the temporal, height, and width components of Qwen2.5-VL's M-RoPE. A content-hashed cache also avoids repeating vision-encoder computation for those segments. In preliminary experiments with Qwen2.5-VL-7B on synthetic needle-in-a-video-haystack questions over public-domain films, the method reduces prefill tokens and end-to-end rebuild latency relative to full recomputation while usually producing the same answer. Densifying the segment containing the answer improves accuracy when that segment is known. When the model selects segments itself, accuracy does not improve: it rarely identifies a needle that was absent from the sparse sample. c5868aa7c101ef8ad7627a0d.title_original: MADJEPA: Enhanced Multi-Stage Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture for Medical Anomaly Detection
c5868aa7c101ef8ad7627a0d.excerpt: arXiv:2611.25194v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Anomaly detection in medical images is a complex task, requiring the development of a robust model using only healthy patient data. fb1b8a0603fcc34fd2a3a31c.title_original: Bradley-Terry Training Can Distort Outcome Probabilities of Initially Accurate Language World Models
fb1b8a0603fcc34fd2a3a31c.excerpt: arXiv:2611.25594v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Comparative feedback, in which a judge says which of two candidate outcomes is closer to what happened, is a practical way to train language world models that assign probabilities to an action's outcomes. On a simulated robot push with enumerated outcome distributions, this objective takes a model that is accurate on unseen layouts (hazard error 2.4 percentage points, pp) and moves 33 to 43 pp of its probability onto outcomes that none of a condition's enumerated branches produces. The cause is the objective, not the comparisons: its optimum, computed before training, predicts where the model ends up, and a likelihood that knows the judge's rule learns from the same comparisons without the shift. The shift is robust: it recurs on unseen conditions, under five candidate laws and a three-fold denser enumeration, and about 29 pp remain without the physically impossible events. Its cost is conditional: with those events it inflates hazard probabilities, and a threshold inherited from the pre-feedback model costs about 3 pp of utility per decision on trained and 1 to 2 pp on unseen conditions, through false rejects; without them the utility loss averages below 1 pp over six seeds, though a small regret in action choice remains. 3e69a81371baf0667bc59b31.title_original: Information Security Risk Preparedness in Electronic Data Interchange: A Comparative Assessment of General IT and Healthcare Environments
3e69a81371baf0667bc59b31.excerpt: arXiv:2611.31294v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Electronic Data Interchange (EDI) supports the exchange of structured information across business and healthcare environments, making information security and organizational risk management critical to reliable digital transactions. A parsimonious regression model incorporating SCP and TP explained 41.6% of the variance in ORTA (R^2 = 0.416, adjusted R^2 = 0.404, p < 0.001). Based on these empirical findings, an EDI Risk Management

fd8fc5925135ecc8f5462345.title_original: Towards Efficient Attack Tree Generation from Attack Graphs for Unobservable Target Analysis
fd8fc5925135ecc8f5462345.excerpt: arXiv:2611.31302v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Attack trees provide a structured approach to security analysis but traditionally require prior knowledge of the attacker's objective. In practice, this objective often remains hidden, even when some attacker actions are partially detected. This paper presents a methodology for generating attack trees without assuming a predefined target by modeling the threat environment as a constraint-weighted graph and applying temporal reachability analysis. The approach identifies probable attacker locations from partial observations and a time budget, carrying traversal cost as an attack-tree attribute. It then extracts target-oriented subgraphs that preserve feasible attack paths while eliminating irrelevant nodes. We demonstrate the framework across three scenarios: a single office building, a multi-building industrial complex, and a real IoT device-communication network recovered from the CICIoT2023 attack dataset. Compared with the baselines, our approach achieves a lower reduction factor while maintaining complete target preservation, substantially outperforming topology-only methods that ignore temporal constraints. We further perform a sensitivity analysis across 66 weight configurations, showing that target identification is stable when strategic value receives at least 20\% of the weight in the single building and at least 50\% in the multi-building complex, while additional experiments reveal sensitivity to perturbations of the

9159e2dca34d1744abf8de3d.title_original: Trustworthy Edge AI: Security, Privacy, and Resilience for Distributed Intelligence
9159e2dca34d1744abf8de3d.excerpt: arXiv:2611.31331v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This chapter examines the principles and emerging research directions for building secure, privacy-preserving, and resilient Edge Artificial Intelligence (Edge AI) systems. As intelligence shifts from centralized clouds to distributed edge environments, challenges arise in ensuring data integrity, privacy, and reliable operation under adversarial and uncertain conditions. The chapter analyzes Edge AI architectures, emphasizing the expanded attack surface due to heterogeneous devices, resource constraints, and dynamic networks. It reviews core security mechanisms, including hardware-rooted trust, zero-trust models, secure communication, and attestation. Privacy-preserving approaches, such as federated learning, secure aggregation, and differential privacy, enable collaborative intelligence without centralized data sharing. Resilience strategies, including fault tolerance, adversarial robustness, and adaptive orchestration, are also explored. Case studies from smart cities, autonomous vehicles, healthcare, and industrial IoT illustrate practical trade-offs. The chapter advocates a holistic, cross-layer design integrating security, privacy, and resilience for trustworthy edge intelligence.

cadc05525333f3cdf14355ec.title_original: High Throughput Meets Low Latency: CKKS Functional Bootstrapping on GPUs
cadc05525333f3cdf14355ec.excerpt: arXiv:2611.31335v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Functional (programmable) bootstrapping extends the bootstrapping operation of Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) to evaluate an arbitrary function while refreshing a ciphertext. This capability was a unique feature of scalar CGGI/DM cryptosystems for many years until it was recently added to the toolset of vectorized FHE schemes, with CKKS being the most promising option both in terms of throughput (amortized time) and functionality. Previous work showed that CKKS functional bootstrapping outperforms CGGI/DM functional bootstrapping in terms of throughput by two to three orders of magnitude, but still loses in latency on CPU by two to three orders of magnitude. We present an optimized GPU implementation of CKKS functional bootstrapping that closes the latency gap. Our implementation supports evaluating functions over both small integers (as in CGGI/DM) and real numbers (unique to CKKS), which we call discrete-CKKS and continuous-CKKS functional bootstrapping, respectively.

0e4f31d53fd49ddeea8bc075.title_original: The Fingerprinting Paradox: Why Sensitivity Undermines Black-Box Model Integrity Verification
0e4f31d53fd49ddeea8bc075.excerpt: arXiv:2611.31455v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Black-box integrity verification aims to detect unauthorized modifications to outsourced models using only prediction APIs. Existing frameworks seek to improve verification efficiency through sensitive fingerprints: queries whose predictions are more likely to change under tampering than those of genuine inputs. We show that this sensitivity can also help dishonest providers recognize verification queries and selectively conceal tampering. We prove that excess sensitivity relative to genuine inputs lower-bounds statistical distinguishability. We evaluate five integrity verification frameworks across three model architectures, three datasets, and three adversarial knowledge settings. When the deployed framework is known, our fingerprint detectors achieve AUCs at least 0.989, and selective filtering makes all five frameworks require significantly larger estimated query budgets than genuine inputs, reversing their intended efficiency advantage. A query-efficiency advantage remains marginally in a small subset of evaluated settings with poor detection transfer. We further design verification methods under stronger concealment constraints but find that reduced detectability comes with losses in sensitivity or fingerprint-generation success. Our results expose a sensitivity-detectability tension and show that sensitivity alone does not ensure efficient black-box verification against adaptive malicious providers.

003cb6061c94a1e7d37835b2.title_original: Aftershock: Yesterday's Linux Kernel Bugs, Tomorrow's Android Exploits
003cb6061c94a1e7d37835b2.excerpt: arXiv:2611.31547v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Android kernels have long suffered from slow patch propagation from Linux upstream, with fixes often reaching devices far later than conventional Linux distributions. Until recently, this lag was largely a patch-management problem. With rapidly improving LLM agents, it is becoming an exploitation problem: public upstream patches can now serve as blueprints for building working n-day exploits before downstream devices are fixed. We test this threat end to end by building an automated pipeline that screens upstream Linux patches, reproduces memory-safety vulnerabilities on Android targets, and drives an LLM agent to construct local privilege escalation exploits from an untrusted application. Across 152 candidate CVEs reported over 33 months, we reproduce 38 vulnerabilities and generate 17 independently verified exploits under production defenses. Exploitation takes a median of 14.3 agent-hours and $321 in API cost, with 90% median reliability; 12 of 14 trials succeed on Pixel 9 and Pixel 10 devices. Notably, the pipeline relies only on publicly available, off-the-shelf models. Surprisingly, only 3 of the 17 exploited CVEs appear in Android Security Bulletins, suggesting limited visibility into which upstream fixes address vulnerabilities that affect Android kernels. For these 17 CVEs, the corresponding upstream patches reach Pixel devices with a median delay of 181 days. Together, these results reveal a stark asymmetry: attackers

e7627d53cc30f47d3f60bdbf.title_original: Evaluating LLM Security Review Agents with Operationally Sourced Ground Truth
e7627d53cc30f47d3f60bdbf.excerpt: arXiv:2611.31606v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM-based security review agents can reason about vulnerabilities that deterministic tools miss, but deploying them responsibly requires knowing whether they actually work. Existing benchmarks construct ground truth synthetically or from public CVE databases and are blind to the vulnerability patterns specific to a given production codebase. We present an evaluation framework grounded in an organisation's own vulnerabilities, with three contributions. First, a dataset construction methodology that derives ground truth from operational security data (bug bounty reports, penetration test findings and internally reported vulnerabilities), exploiting the property that a confirmed vulnerability must exist immediately before its fix is merged and be absent immediately after. Second, two complementary evaluation strategies: one reviewing the pull request that introduced a vulnerability and one searching a repository where it already exists. Both run through a two-agent pipeline pairing a Security Engineer agent, which reviews code without knowledge of the vulnerability, with a Judge agent that decides whether its findings would have mitigated the known issue. Third, a trace-level behavioural characterisation of how frontier models reason about these vulnerabilities. Across GPT-5.5, Sonnet 4.6 and Opus 4.7, GPT-5.5 shows higher discovery rates on the pull-request strategy (57%, 95% CI [42%, 72%]) after a round of OPRO-style improvements

bb4aeb24611b6859e059c2e7.title_original: Internal inconsistencies and unresolved experimental evidence in a quantum neurosecurity framework
bb4aeb24611b6859e059c2e7.excerpt: arXiv:2611.31622v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This article presents a technical and theoretical assessment of the Quantum-Entangled Neuro-Symbolic Swarm Federation (QENSSF), a framework intended for privacy-preserving, quantum-secure, AI-powered, multimodal healthcare data analysis, introduced by Ben Othman and Ali (2025). They claim QENSSF is a first-in-class framework with provable privacy and security guarantees, support these with theorems and proofs, report an experimental evaluation on IBM's quantum Eagle processor, report a real-world quantum key distribution (QKD) test, and claim use of real-world multimodal datasets (ADNI, UK Biobank, and MIMIC-IV). Our examination of quantitative support for these claims identified various concerns. Most importantly, the security criterion of a central guarantee (Theorem 1) cannot be satisfied given the risk formulation and relevant constraints, which, along with calculation errors in the proof, directly undermines the claim of provable security. Furthermore, insufficient reporting of biomedical datasets and unresolved discrepancies in the hardware evaluation limit verification of the experimental claims and overall reproducibility. QENSSF identifies a real need: ensuring privacy and security of healthcare data while patients benefit from AI-powered analysis. This need is particularly pressing for sensitive neural data, including the neuroimaging data available through sources such as ADNI. Privacy concerns also extend to wearable

14f529b449b7b66b8db593a2.title_original: Open-Set Radio Frequency Fingerprint Identification with Feature Fusion and Vision Transformer
14f529b449b7b66b8db593a2.excerpt: arXiv:2611.31636v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Radio frequency fingerprint identification (RFFI) is a promising device authentication technique for the Internet of Things (IoT) that leverages hardware impairments to uniquely identify devices. We built a testbed involving ten legitimate LoRa devices and five rogue devices. We conducted a comprehensive experimental evaluation and compared our approach with several benchmark algorithms. bdcfb4f6aa0bcb399973da48.title_original: Harvesting Apple's Orchard: A Security Analysis of On-Device CoreML Models Across the Apple Ecosystem
bdcfb4f6aa0bcb399973da48.excerpt: arXiv:2611.31688v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Apple ships hundreds of task-specific machine-learning models inside iOS, iPadOS, macOS, and tvOS. f144db85f23787c5c6e93e52.title_original: SigK: rPPG-based key agreement scheme for mHealth
f144db85f23787c5c6e93e52.excerpt: arXiv:2611.31721v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As mobile health advances, the use of biomedical sensors for disease monitoring, diagnosis, and treatment is increasing. These sensors often need to be connected through wireless communication technologies to process physiological information from various body parts effectively. Since the data transmitted in these devices usually contain sensitive personal medical information, it is crucial to establish secure communication between devices. They can be extracted from physiological signals such as photoplethysmogram (PPG) or electrocardiogram (ECG), allowing key agreement schemes without pre-key distribution. However, traditional solutions are based on contact measurement devices (e.g., wristbands, chest straps), which limit their applicability in contactless healthcare scenarios. In this paper, we propose a remote PPG-based key agreement scheme to facilitate secure communication between contactless medical devices. We leverage medical devices equipped with cameras to capture remote PPG signals from human faces, and then utilize the signal's power spectral density and peak-peak interval to establish a key agreement with signals synchronously acquired in the Body Area Network (BAN). 28baf21f3765fcdd7ec53e8b.title_original: Mixed-Initiative Mining of Root-Cause Analyses into Audit Priors for C/C++ Vulnerability Hunting
28baf21f3765fcdd7ec53e8b.excerpt: arXiv:2611.31744v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Vulnerability auditing of large C/C++ codebases is constrained by limited review attention. Human auditors and LLM-based agents need operational priors that indicate where to look first and what to suspect, but such priors are rarely available in directly usable form. Rather than proposing a new vulnerability detector, we derive audit-steering artifacts from evidence-backed root-cause analysis (RCA) reports. We introduce two complementary representations: Occurrence Context (OC), a location prior based on file role, function role, and data-structure class; and Vulnerability-Inducing Structural Patterns (VISP), reusable failure-mechanism priors. OC guides where to inspect, while VISP guides what to suspect. On 108 CVEs from Vul4C, OC's parser-based priority ranking, without LLM inference, outperforms generic prioritization baselines with moderate-to-large effect sizes. Packaged as executable SKILLs, OC and VISP form a dual-SKILL workflow that improves audit-relevant broad coverage, defined as match-or-partial findings within ground-truth functions that share the patch's failure mechanism, as assessed by three LLM judges. Across the 108-CVE cohort, dual-SKILL improves function-level broad matches by 5.3 percentage points; gains reach 7.2 points on mid-size projects and 15.0 points on large (1500-4999-line) vulnerable files. These results suggest that RCA-derived priors help direct limited audit attention toward vulnerable code. Th

c493358d5495c7efa40364d1.title_original: Separating Measurement Failures from Defence Failures in Split Language-Model Privacy
c493358d5495c7efa40364d1.excerpt: arXiv:2611.31752v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Split-training privacy evaluations fail through distinct mechanisms. Evaluators can overlook an exposed gradient channel, align reconstructions against shifted labels, or deploy uncalibrated probes before testing a candidate defence, while calibrated attacks can also refute real defences. Separating these failure modes alters which claims survive. 1667721de68a8c4d9a1953fd.title_original: HDMark: Holographic Multi-Bit Model Watermarking for Intellectual Property Protection in Hyperdimensional Computing
1667721de68a8c4d9a1953fd.excerpt: arXiv:2611.31781v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hyperdimensional computing (HDC) models deployed on edge hardware are valuable intellectual property that is easy to steal, since a trained classifier consolidates its learned knowledge into a compact set of class prototype hypervectors; yet protecting their ownership through watermarking remains largely unexplored. HDMark maps a multi-bit owner identity to secret quasi-orthogonal carriers, superimposes them holographically onto the trained class prototypes, and verifies ownership with a statistical test. Across four datasets and three HDC learning rules, HDMark leaves accuracy essentially unchanged and verifies a 64-bit identity in 99.8% of trials at p < 0.001. We derive closed-form expressions for prediction fidelity and bit recovery that match measurements within 0.4 pp mean absolute error. The watermark survives fine-tuning and low-bit quantization, while attempting to erase it through noise injection, pruning, or overwriting severely degrades model accuracy. We further identify a dimension-permutation attack specific to HDC, which reorders hypervector coordinates to evade verification without altering predictions, and counter it through encoder realignment. 4aebd803dfd9c578174b3587.title_original: SwarmLeak: Does Coordination Improve Privacy Attacks on LLM Agents?
4aebd803dfd9c578174b3587.excerpt: arXiv:2611.31791v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM agents increasingly collaborate in group chats while holding tool access to confidential records, which makes the shared chat an attack surface. It remains unclear whether several colluding attackers extract such information more effectively than one. We introduce SwarmLeak, a red-teaming dataset of 24 synthetic group-chat scenarios across healthcare, law, finance, and software engineering, where attackers pose as colleagues to make a victim agent post protected fields despite an explicit confidentiality policy. With GLM 5.2 attacking five victim models through seven conversational strategies, we compare one attacker with a swarm of four sharing a private channel, matching scenarios, strategies, and a 200,000-token budget that also covers swarm coordination. Swarms show no advantage: a single attacker matches or exceeds them on every victim, and the share of runs leaking any field differs between conditions by at most 14.3 percentage points, whereas changing the victim shifts it from 0% to 99.4%. On the two most vulnerable models, nearly every run leaks under both conditions, but single attackers expose more of the record at first disclosure (85.4% vs. 68.1% of protected fields on Nemotron 3.5 Lightning). 0e20e8d50abab57e2327960d.title_original: Where Did My Tokens Go? Verifiable Token Billing for LLM Services
0e20e8d50abab57e2327960d.excerpt: arXiv:2611.31806v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Users of large language model (LLM) services receive token bills with limited evidence of which calls incurred their charges. In broker-mediated agent workflows, calls arise after authorization and billing evidence spans service domains. A bill can count one genuine receipt twice and omit another. Valid metering evidence can also be attributed to the wrong execution. We present \textsc{TokenProv}, which uses authenticated provider acceptances to establish settlement coverage and verify token charges. An authenticated causal history links runtime attempts to the signed policy, and jointly signed handoffs bind intent, dispatch, and acceptance to the same call. Handoffs submitted independently of the bill can reveal omitted calls. The auditor requires a one-to-one match between observable acceptances and settled receipts. For each acceptance, a common provider relation binds metered usage to the cache-dependent execution of the accepted input using the registered model and serving rules, and checks the charge under the pricing rule. To limit serving-path overhead, providers can use attested state transitions in trusted execution environments or defer proof generation until audit by committing to witnesses in receipts before settlement. The auditor recomputes the bill from the verified charges. We prove audit soundness relative to authenticated evidence. 40de85c5e8603e0b5b225757.title_original: The Oracle Is Not Enough: Secure Settlement for Prediction Markets
40de85c5e8603e0b5b225757.excerpt: arXiv:2611.31866v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Prediction markets are becoming an important mechanism for aggregating information and forecasting uncertain real-world events. As they grow in scale and value, reliable settlement becomes critical because settlement determines the winning outcome and allocation of market collateral. Yet many heterogeneous markets require market-specific evidence and interpretation, and incorrect settlement can create direct financial incentives for manipulation. In this paper, we ask how to settle heterogeneous markets correctly and efficiently at scale. We first compare existing settlement designs in their support for heterogeneous markets, reliance on direct operator intervention, and resistance to manipulation, motivating a layered architecture that combines incentivized crowdsourcing with stake-backed voting and selective post-settlement review. Building on this architecture, we develop a stake-backed settlement protocol that provides economic security and settlement liveness under market-specific verification costs. Specifically, we prove that manipulation is unprofitable for every settled market and give two constructions that support sufficient self-enforcing participation with controlled reward expenditure. Using historical Polymarket and UMA data, we evaluate the protocol under real-world conditions. We find that 99% of admitted markets can be settled with modest participation rewards even under high verification costs.

06c594c5657d7d53a6b43076.title_original: MALET & Katalina: A Large-Scale Dataset and Static Analysis of macOS Malware
06c594c5657d7d53a6b43076.excerpt: arXiv:2611.31949v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: While malware on platforms such as Windows and Android has been extensively studied, the macOS ecosystem remains comparatively understudied.
